wobbly.example: After the long ride, my legs felt wobbly.
wobbly.whyHard: This word is harder than everyday English.

wolf.meaning: Wild animals that look like large dogs and hunt in a group.
wolf.whyHard: This word is less common than the school words for the same idea.

wonder.usageNote: A very useful word. Learn it.

wonder.whyHard: This word is harder than everyday English.

wooden.usageNote: A common word. Good to know.
wooden.example: We sat on a wooden bench.
wooden.whyHard: This word is harder than everyday English.

work.meaning: To do a job; also, to go or act in the right way, like a machine that works.

senses.meaning: To use something and make it act, like magic.
senses.whyHard: Not the usual meaning! Usually: To do a job.

anchors.context: So can anybody work the spell?

senses.meaning: Old and thin because it has been used a lot.

anchors.context: The leather was smooth and worn.

wow.meaning: A word you say when you are very surprised or think something is great.
wow.usageNote: A common word. Good to know.
wow.whyHard: This word is harder than everyday English.

wrap.usageNote: A common word. Good to learn.
wrap.example: She wrapped the gift in red paper.
wrap.whyHard: This word is harder than everyday English.

wrinkled.meaning: With many small lines on it, like old skin.
wrinkled.usageNote: A common word. Good to know.
wrinkled.whyHard: This word is harder than everyday English.

yank.whyHard: This word is harder than everyday English.

yard.meaning: The open ground around a house.
yard.whyHard: This word is less common than the school words for the same idea.

yay.meaning: A word you shout when you are happy.
yay.usageNote: You do not need to learn it now. It is a word for this story.
yay.whyHard: This word is harder than everyday English.

yeah.usageNote: A common word. Good to know.
yeah.whyHard: This word is harder than everyday English.

yell.usageNote: A common word. Good to know.
yell.whyHard: This word is harder than everyday English.

yep.whyHard: This word is harder than everyday English.

yikes.meaning: A word you say when you are suddenly surprised or afraid.
yikes.usageNote: You do not need to learn it now. It is a word for this story.
yikes.whyHard: This word is harder than everyday English.

zigzag.usageNote: You only need to understand it in this book.

paragraphs.context: “Yeah, sure,” said Jack. “A real monster in
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack does not believe Annie. There are no monsters in his town.
paragraphs.simple: "Yes, of course," Jack says. "A real monster in our town." He does not believe her.
paragraphs.tone: Jack does not mean "yes". He is saying the opposite, because he thinks Annie is being silly.

background.note: Frog Creek is the small town where Jack and Annie live. It is not a real town. Pennsylvania is a real state in the east of the USA.

paragraphs.context: Annie loved pretend stuff. But Jack was eight
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie and Jack are very different: she loves games of make-believe, and he likes real things.
paragraphs.simple: Annie loved to play games that were not real. But Jack was eight and a half years old, and he liked real things.
paragraphs.tone: The writer shows us the two children: Annie is wild and full of ideas, Jack is careful and serious.

paragraphs.context: Jack left the road and headed into the
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack goes into the woods to look for Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Jack left the road and went into the woods. The late-afternoon sun made the trees look gold.

paragraphs.context: There she was. Standing under a tall oak
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie shows Jack a rope ladder under a tall tree.
paragraphs.simple: There she was, under a tall oak tree. "Look," she said, and she pointed at a ladder made of rope.

paragraphs.context: There—at the top—was a tree house. It was
paragraphs.mainIdea: At the top of the ladder there is a tree house.
paragraphs.simple: At the top of the tree there was a tree house. It sat safely between two branches.

paragraphs.context: He pushed his glasses into place. He gripped
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack loves books, so he climbs up after Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Jack pushed his glasses into the right place. He held the sides of the rope ladder tightly and climbed up.

paragraphs.context: Wow. The tree house was filled with books.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The tree house is full of old and new books.
paragraphs.simple: The tree house was full of books, everywhere. Some were very old, with dusty covers. Some were new, with bright, shiny covers.

paragraphs.context: Jack looked out the window with her. Down
paragraphs.mainIdea: From the tree house, Jack can see his whole town.
paragraphs.simple: Jack looked out of the window with Annie. Below them were the tops of the other trees. Far away he could see the town library, the primary school and the park.

background.note: In the USA, children go to elementary school from about age 6 to 11. It is like primary school in China.

paragraphs.context: Sure enough. There was their white wooden house
paragraphs.mainIdea: They can see their own house and the dog next door.
paragraphs.simple: Yes, it was true. There was their white wooden house with a green porch. Next door was Henry, the neighbors' black dog. He looked very small from so high up.

background.note: Many American houses have a porch: a covered area by the front door where people can sit.

paragraphs.context: But even as he said this, Jack opened
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack knows they should not touch the books, but he opens the dinosaur book.
paragraphs.simple: At the same time as he said this, Jack opened the dinosaur book at the bookmark. He could not stop himself.
paragraphs.tone: Jack says one thing but does another. This is funny, and it shows how much he loves books.

paragraphs.context: He turned to a picture of an ancient
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack sees a picture of a Pteranodon, a flying reptile from long ago.
paragraphs.simple: He turned to a picture of a flying reptile from very long ago. It was a Pteranodon.

background.note: A Pteranodon was a big flying reptile that lived at the time of the dinosaurs, about 85 million years ago. It was not a bird and not a dinosaur.

paragraphs.context: Jack studied the picture of the odd-looking creature
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack looks closely at the strange flying animal in the picture.
paragraphs.simple: Jack looked carefully at the picture of the strange-looking animal flying through the sky.

paragraphs.context: A giant creature was gliding above the treetops!
paragraphs.mainIdea: A real Pteranodon is flying above the trees.
paragraphs.simple: A giant animal was flying smoothly above the trees! He had a long, strange crest on the back of his head, a thin beak and huge wings like a bat's.

paragraphs.context: The creature curved through the sky. He was
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Pteranodon flies straight toward the tree house.
paragraphs.simple: The animal flew in a curve through the sky. He was flying straight to the tree house. He looked like a plane with no engine.

background.note: A glider is a light plane with no engine. It flies on the wind, like the Pteranodon.

paragraphs.context: Suddenly the creature soared up. High into the
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Pteranodon flies high, and Jack almost falls out of the window.
paragraphs.simple: Suddenly the animal flew up, high into the sky. Jack almost fell out of the window when he tried to see it.

paragraphs.context: Jack opened his eyes. Sunlight slanted through the
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack opens his eyes. Everything looks the same inside, but something has changed.
paragraphs.simple: Jack opened his eyes. Sunlight came through the window at an angle.

paragraphs.context: The Pteranodon was soaring through the sky. The
paragraphs.mainIdea: Outside is a land from long ago, just like in the picture.
paragraphs.simple: The Pteranodon was flying high in the sky. The ground was covered with ferns and tall grass. There was a river that turned this way and that, a hill, and volcanoes far away.

paragraphs.context: The Pteranodon glided down to the base of
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Pteranodon lands and stands still at the bottom of their tree.
paragraphs.simple: The Pteranodon flew smoothly down to the bottom of their tree. He slowed down, stopped and stood very still.

paragraphs.context: Jack looked out the window with her. The
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Pteranodon stands under the tree like a guard.
paragraphs.simple: Jack looked out of the window too. The Pteranodon stood at the bottom of the oak tree, like a guard. His giant wings were open on both sides of him.

paragraphs.context: This flying reptile lived in the Cretaceous period.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The book says the Pteranodon lived 65 million years ago.
paragraphs.simple: This flying reptile lived in the Cretaceous period. There have been no Pteranodons for 65 million years.

background.note: The Cretaceous period was a long time in the history of the earth, about 145 to 66 million years ago. Many dinosaurs lived then.

paragraphs.context: Annie dropped to the ground. She stepped boldly
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie goes down and walks bravely up to the Pteranodon.
paragraphs.simple: Annie jumped down to the ground. She walked bravely up to the very old animal.

paragraphs.context: Oh, brother. She was always trying to make
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie always wants to be friends with animals, but this time Jack thinks it is too much.
paragraphs.simple: Oh no. Annie always tried to be friends with animals. But this time she was doing too much. It was not safe.
paragraphs.tone: "Oh, brother" shows that Jack is tired of Annie's wild ideas.

paragraphs.context: Jack took a deep breath. Okay. He would
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack decides to go down and study the animal like a scientist.
paragraphs.simple: Jack took a deep breath. OK. He would go down too. He could look carefully at the animal and write notes, like a scientist.
paragraphs.tone: Jack is afraid, but he makes himself brave by thinking like a scientist.

paragraphs.context: Jack stepped forward. He put out his arm.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack slowly and carefully touches the Pteranodon.
paragraphs.simple: Jack stepped forward and put out his arm, very carefully. He moved his hand down the animal's neck.

paragraphs.context: Interesting. A thin layer of fuzz covered the
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Pteranodon's skin is covered with thin, soft hair.
paragraphs.simple: How interesting! A thin coat of soft hair covered the Pteranodon's skin.

paragraphs.context: Jack looked at the Pteranodon again. The creature
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Pteranodon has a long, hard crest on its head.
paragraphs.simple: Jack looked at the Pteranodon again. It had a hard crest of bone on top of its head. The crest was longer than Jack's arm.

paragraphs.context: The creature fixed his eyes on Annie. His
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Pteranodon looks at Annie and opens and closes its long mouth.
paragraphs.simple: The animal looked hard at Annie. His long jaws opened and closed, like a giant pair of scissors.

paragraphs.context: “Quit it!” she said. But she started up
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie climbs up quickly, and Jack hurries after her.
paragraphs.simple: "Stop it!" Annie said. But she started up the ladder. Jack climbed quickly after her, using his hands and feet.

paragraphs.context: They were panting as they looked out the
paragraphs.mainIdea: From the tree house they watch a dinosaur on the hill.
paragraphs.simple: They were breathing fast as they looked out of the window at the dinosaur. He stood on top of the hill and ate flowers from a tree.

paragraphs.context: The dinosaur looked like a huge rhinoceros. Only
paragraphs.mainIdea: The dinosaur looks like a rhino with three horns.
paragraphs.simple: The dinosaur looked like a huge rhino, but he had three horns, not one. Two long horns were above his eyes and one was on his nose. Behind his head was a big thing like a shield.

background.note: A rhinoceros (rhino) is a big, heavy animal from Africa or Asia with one or two horns on its nose.

paragraphs.context: The Triceratops lived in the late Cretaceous period.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The book says the Triceratops ate only plants.
paragraphs.simple: The Triceratops lived late in the Cretaceous period. This dinosaur ate plants and was more than 12,000 pounds, about 5,400 kilos.

background.note: Triceratops means "three-horned face". It was a big plant-eating dinosaur.

paragraphs.context: He shoved the dinosaur book into his pack.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack puts the book in his pack and goes down the ladder.
paragraphs.simple: He pushed the dinosaur book into his pack. He put the pack over his shoulder and started down the ladder.

paragraphs.context: When he reached the bottom of the hill,
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack hides behind a bush at the bottom of the hill.
paragraphs.simple: When he got to the bottom of the hill, he went down on his knees behind a big bush.

paragraphs.context: The dinosaur was incredibly big. Bigger than a
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Triceratops is bigger than a truck.
paragraphs.simple: The dinosaur was very, very big, bigger than a truck. He was eating the flowers from a magnolia tree.

paragraphs.context: Annie pointed to herself. She walked her fingers
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie tells Jack without words that she wants to go to the dinosaur.
paragraphs.simple: Annie pointed to herself. She "walked" her fingers through the air. She pointed to the dinosaur and smiled.
paragraphs.tone: Annie cannot talk, because Jack said "Shush!". So she uses her hands to say "I am going to walk to him."

paragraphs.context: Too late. The big dinosaur had spotted Annie.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Triceratops sees Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Too late. The big dinosaur had seen Annie. He looked down at her from the top of the hill, with half a flower in his mouth.

paragraphs.context: But the Triceratops just gazed calmly down at
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Triceratops does not hurt Annie. He walks away.
paragraphs.simple: But the Triceratops just looked down calmly at Annie. Then he turned and ran away with long, easy steps, down the side of the hill.

paragraphs.context: As Jack started after Annie, he saw something
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack finds something shiny in the grass.
paragraphs.simple: Jack started to follow Annie. Then he saw something shining in the tall grass. He picked it up.

paragraphs.context: A letter was engraved on the medallion. A
paragraphs.mainIdea: There is a fancy letter M on the medallion.
paragraphs.simple: A letter was cut into the medallion. It was a beautiful M.

paragraphs.context: Clutching her magnolia flower, she took off down
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie runs down the other side of the hill with her flower.
paragraphs.simple: Holding her magnolia flower tightly, she ran down the hill.

paragraphs.context: Jack heard another sound as well. A deep,
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack hears a deep, loud sound.
paragraphs.simple: Jack heard another sound too: a deep, loud sound, like a tuba.

background.note: A tuba is a very big metal music instrument. It makes a very deep, low sound.

paragraphs.context: The valley below was filled with nests. Big
paragraphs.mainIdea: The valley is full of nests with baby dinosaurs.
paragraphs.simple: The valley below was full of nests. They were big nests made of mud. And the nests were full of tiny dinosaurs!

paragraphs.context: Annie was crouching next to one of the
paragraphs.mainIdea: A huge mother dinosaur is standing over Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie was low on the ground next to a nest. A huge dinosaur with a mouth like a duck's was standing over her!

background.note: Some dinosaurs had a wide, flat mouth like a duck's bill (the hard mouth of a bird). People call them duck-billed dinosaurs.

paragraphs.context: The huge dinosaur was towering above Annie. Waving
paragraphs.mainIdea: The mother dinosaur waves her arms and makes her loud sound.
paragraphs.simple: The huge dinosaur was standing high above Annie. She was waving her arms and making her tuba sound.

paragraphs.context: Jack inched farther down the hill. Until he
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack slowly moves closer to Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Jack moved down the hill very slowly, a little at a time, until he was just one arm away from Annie.

paragraphs.context: “You have to use your brain,” said Jack.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack tells Annie to think before she acts.
paragraphs.simple: "You have to think," said Jack. "You can't just run to a nest of babies. There is always a mother near them."

paragraphs.context: The Anatosauruses lived in colonies. While a few
paragraphs.mainIdea: The book says these dinosaurs lived in big groups and took turns.
paragraphs.simple: The Anatosauruses lived in big groups. Some mothers watched the nests while others went to find food.

background.note: Anatosaurus was a big duck-billed dinosaur that ate plants. The name means "duck lizard".

paragraphs.context: An enormous ugly monster was coming across the
paragraphs.mainIdea: A huge, ugly monster is walking across the flat land.
paragraphs.simple: A very big, ugly monster was coming across the flat land.

paragraphs.context: He was walking on two big legs. And
paragraphs.mainIdea: The monster walks on two legs and has tiny arms.
paragraphs.simple: He walked on two big legs. He swung a long, thick tail, and his two tiny arms hung down.

paragraphs.context: “Tyrannosaurus rex!” whispered Jack.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The monster is a Tyrannosaurus rex.
paragraphs.simple: "Tyrannosaurus rex!" Jack said quietly.

background.note: Tyrannosaurus rex (T. rex) was one of the biggest meat-eating dinosaurs. It had huge jaws and very long teeth. "Rex" means "king".

paragraphs.context: They dashed down the hill together. Through the
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack and Annie run back to the tree house.
paragraphs.simple: They ran fast down the hill together: through the tall grass, through the ferns, past the Pteranodon, and straight to the rope ladder.

paragraphs.context: But now the valley below was filled with
paragraphs.mainIdea: Now the valley is full of mother dinosaurs guarding the nests.
paragraphs.simple: But now the valley below was full of Anatosauruses. They all stood around the nests to keep them safe.

paragraphs.context: He charged down the hill. He leaped to
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack runs down, grabs his pack and the book.
paragraphs.simple: He ran fast down the hill. He jumped to his backpack and picked it up quickly. He took the dinosaur book.

paragraphs.context: The Tyrannosaurus rex was back! And he was
paragraphs.mainIdea: The T. rex is between Jack and the tree house.
paragraphs.simple: The Tyrannosaurus rex was back! And he was standing between Jack and the tree house!

paragraphs.context: His heart was beating so fast he could
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack is so afraid that he cannot think.
paragraphs.simple: His heart was beating very fast, so he almost could not think.

paragraphs.context: He peeked out at the giant monster. The
paragraphs.mainIdea: The T. rex has huge, sharp teeth.
paragraphs.simple: He looked out from behind the tree at the giant monster. The horrible animal was opening and closing his huge jaws. His teeth were as big as big kitchen knives.

paragraphs.context: Tyrannosaurus rex was the largest meat-eating land animal
paragraphs.mainIdea: The book says the T. rex could eat a person in one bite.
paragraphs.simple: Tyrannosaurus rex was the biggest meat-eating animal on land ever. If it were alive today, it could eat a person in one bite.

paragraphs.context: Okay. He couldn’t hide on the other side
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack thinks about what he can do. Each idea is dangerous.
paragraphs.simple: He could not hide on the other side of the hill, because the Anatosauruses might all run in fear and step on him.

paragraphs.context: She went straight to the Pteranodon. She was
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie is "talking" to the Pteranodon and pointing at Jack.
paragraphs.simple: She went straight to the Pteranodon. She was talking to him and moving her arms like wings. She pointed at Jack, at the sky and at the tree house.
paragraphs.tone: Annie is asking the Pteranodon for help. Jack does not understand this yet, so he thinks she is crazy.

paragraphs.context: Just then a giant shadow covered Jack. He
paragraphs.mainIdea: Suddenly a big shadow covers Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Just then a giant shadow covered Jack. He looked up.

paragraphs.context: The Pteranodon was gliding overhead. The giant creature
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Pteranodon flies down to Jack.
paragraphs.simple: The Pteranodon was flying above him. The giant animal flew smoothly down to the top of the hill.

paragraphs.context: Jack put his book in his pack. Then
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack gets onto the Pteranodon's back.
paragraphs.simple: Jack put his book in his pack. Then he slowly and carefully sat down on the Pteranodon's back.

paragraphs.context: The creature moved forward. He spread out his
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Pteranodon takes off with Jack on his back.
paragraphs.simple: The animal moved forward. He opened his wings and went up into the air!

paragraphs.context: They teetered this way. Then that.
paragraphs.mainIdea: At first they move from side to side.
paragraphs.simple: They moved this way, then that way, as if they would fall.

paragraphs.context: Then the Pteranodon soared out over the plain—over
paragraphs.mainIdea: They fly over the plain and the Triceratops.
paragraphs.simple: Then the Pteranodon flew out high over the flat land, over the Triceratops that was eating grass.

paragraphs.context: It was amazing! It was a miracle!
paragraphs.mainIdea: The ride is wonderful.
paragraphs.simple: It was wonderful! It was like magic!
paragraphs.tone: These short, happy lines show how Jack feels: free and excited.

paragraphs.context: The wind was rushing through his hair. The
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack feels the wind and smells the fresh air.
paragraphs.simple: The wind was moving fast through his hair. The air smelled sweet and fresh.

paragraphs.context: Jack couldn’t believe it. He was riding on
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack cannot believe he is riding a flying reptile.
paragraphs.simple: Jack could not believe it. He was riding on the back of a flying reptile from long, long ago!

paragraphs.context: Suddenly something slammed against the oak tree. The
paragraphs.mainIdea: The T. rex hits the tree, and the tree house shakes.
paragraphs.simple: Suddenly something hit the oak tree hard. The tree house shook like a leaf in the wind.

paragraphs.context: He grabbed it and tore through it, looking
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack looks fast through the Pennsylvania book.
paragraphs.simple: He took it and turned the pages very fast. He was looking for the photo of the Frog Creek woods.

paragraphs.context: The woods were lit with a golden late-afternoon
paragraphs.mainIdea: They are home, and no time has passed.
paragraphs.simple: The woods had the same gold, late-afternoon light. The sun was going to go down soon.

paragraphs.context: Jack still felt dazed. He just stared at
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack is still surprised and cannot think clearly.
paragraphs.simple: Jack still could not think clearly. He just looked at Annie.

paragraphs.context: “Oh, look,” said Jack. “I almost forgot about
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack shows Annie the gold medallion with the letter M.
paragraphs.simple: "Oh, look," said Jack. "I almost forgot this." He took the gold medallion out of his pocket. "Someone lost this in dinosaur land. Look, there's a letter M on it."

paragraphs.context: As they walked past all the houses on
paragraphs.mainIdea: At home, the trip starts to feel like a dream.
paragraphs.simple: As they walked past the houses on their street, the trip to the time of the dinosaurs really did seem more and more like a dream.

paragraphs.context: He felt the engraving of the letter M.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack touches the M, and his fingers feel strange.
paragraphs.simple: He felt the letter M cut into the medallion. It made Jack's fingers feel a little sharp and light, like small electric shocks.

paragraphs.context: He couldn’t explain what had happened today. But
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack knows the trip was real.
paragraphs.simple: He could not explain what had happened today. But he was sure that their trip in the magic tree house was real.

paragraphs.context: Yesterday so many strange things had happened. Now
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack cannot sleep. He is thinking about yesterday.
paragraphs.simple: Yesterday many strange things happened. Now he was trying to understand them.

paragraphs.context: Not his mom. Or his dad. Or his
paragraphs.mainIdea: No one will believe Jack's story, only Annie.
paragraphs.simple: His mom will not believe it. His dad will not believe it. His teacher, Ms. Watkins, will not believe it. Only Annie will. She went with him to the time of the dinosaurs.

background.note: In American schools, children in the third grade are about 8 or 9 years old.

paragraphs.context: “I don’t think we should,” said Jack. He
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack is afraid the magic person may be unkind.
paragraphs.simple: "I don't think we should," said Jack. He was worried. What if the "magic person" was not nice? What if he or she did not want children to know about the tree house?

paragraphs.context: Jack put on jeans, a warm sweatshirt, and
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack gets dressed and packs his bag.
paragraphs.simple: Jack put on jeans, a warm sweatshirt and sports shoes. He threw his notebook and pencil into his backpack.

background.note: Sneakers are soft sports shoes. British people call them trainers.

paragraphs.context: Annie was waiting by the back door. She
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie has a flashlight and calls it a magic wand.
paragraphs.simple: Annie was waiting by the back door. She shone a flashlight in Jack's face. "Ta-da! A magic wand!" she said.
paragraphs.tone: "Ta-da!" is what a magician says when he shows a trick. Annie is playing.

background.note: People say "Ta-da!" when they show something with a big surprise, like at the end of a magic trick.

paragraphs.context: They slipped out the door into the cool
paragraphs.mainIdea: They go out quietly into the early morning.
paragraphs.simple: They went quietly out of the door into the cool early-morning air. Small insects were singing. The dog next door barked.

paragraphs.context: Step by step, she and Jack walked between
paragraphs.mainIdea: They walk slowly through the dark woods.
paragraphs.simple: Step by step, she and Jack walked between the trees. Jack stopped breathing for a moment. The dark woods were scary.

paragraphs.context: There it was. The mysterious tree house. At
paragraphs.mainIdea: They find the tree house again.
paragraphs.simple: There it was: the strange tree house, at the top of the tallest tree in the woods.

paragraphs.context: He started up the ladder. When he was
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack climbs up as the sun begins to come up.
paragraphs.simple: He started up the ladder. When he was almost at the tree house, he saw light far away in the sky. The day was starting.

paragraphs.context: The light was shining on a book about
paragraphs.mainIdea: The light shines on a book about knights and castles.
paragraphs.simple: The light was on a book about knights and castles. There was a blue leather bookmark in it.

paragraphs.context: A knight in shining armor! Riding a black
paragraphs.mainIdea: A knight in armor is riding through their woods.
paragraphs.simple: A knight in shining armor! He was riding a black horse through the Frog Creek woods!

background.note: Knights were soldiers in Europe about 500 to 1,000 years ago. They rode horses and wore metal armor. Today, "a knight in shining armor" also means a person who comes to save you.

paragraphs.context: Jack opened his eyes. He shivered. The air
paragraphs.mainIdea: They are in a new place. It is cold and wet.
paragraphs.simple: Jack opened his eyes. He was shaking a little. The air was wet and cool.

paragraphs.context: A huge castle loomed out of the fog.
paragraphs.mainIdea: A huge castle comes out of the fog.
paragraphs.simple: A huge castle came into view, big and dark, out of the fog.

paragraphs.context: Jack groaned. Okay, she had won. He couldn’t
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack goes after Annie. He also wants to look.
paragraphs.simple: Jack made an unhappy sound. OK, she had won. He could not leave without her. And he also wanted to have a quick look a little himself.
paragraphs.tone: Jack says he is unhappy, but secretly he wants an adventure too.

paragraphs.context: This is a knight arriving for a castle
paragraphs.mainIdea: The book tells about knights and their heavy armor.
paragraphs.simple: This is a knight who is coming to a big castle meal. Knights wore armor when they went on long, dangerous trips. The armor was very heavy. Just a helmet could be up to forty pounds, about 18 kilos.

background.note: In the time of knights, a lord had big meals with many kinds of food in his castle. Many people came, and there was music and fun.

paragraphs.context: Wow. Jack had weighed forty pounds when he
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack thinks about how heavy a helmet is.
paragraphs.simple: Wow. Jack was forty pounds when he was five years old. So it would be like riding a horse with a five-year-old child on your head.
paragraphs.tone: Jack makes a funny picture to understand the weight.

paragraphs.context: A drawbridge crossed the moat. The moat was
paragraphs.mainIdea: The book tells about the drawbridge and the moat.
paragraphs.simple: A bridge that can be pulled up went over the moat. The moat was full of water, to help keep enemies out of the castle. Some people think there were crocodiles in the moat.

background.note: A drawbridge is a bridge that people can pull up with chains, so enemies cannot cross.

paragraphs.context: A piercing shriek split the air.
paragraphs.mainIdea: They hear a loud scream.
paragraphs.simple: A loud, high scream suddenly broke the quiet.

paragraphs.context: The hawk house was in the inner ward
paragraphs.mainIdea: The book tells about the hawk house.
paragraphs.simple: The hawk house was in the inner area of the castle. People trained hawks to catch other birds and small animals.

background.note: In the time of knights, rich people trained hawks to hunt for them. This sport is called falconry. The birds lived in a hawk house.

paragraphs.context: He pointed to a picture of a big
paragraphs.mainIdea: The book shows a big party in the castle.
paragraphs.simple: He pointed to a picture of a big party. Men stood by the door and played drums and horns.

paragraphs.context: Fanfares were played to announce different dishes in
paragraphs.mainIdea: The book says music was played for each new food.
paragraphs.simple: Short, loud music was played to tell people that a new kind of food was coming. Feasts were held in the Great Hall.

background.note: The Great Hall was the biggest room in a castle. People ate, met and had parties there.

paragraphs.context: “Wait,” said Jack, studying the picture. It showed
paragraphs.mainIdea: In the picture boys carry whole pigs, pies and even peacocks.
paragraphs.simple: It showed boys of Jack's age carrying big plates of food: whole pigs, pies, and peacocks with all their feathers. Peacocks?
paragraphs.tone: Jack is surprised that people ate peacocks.

background.note: At big feasts long ago, cooks sometimes cooked a peacock and then put its beautiful feathers back on, to make it look alive.

paragraphs.context: He saw Annie dashing across the real drawbridge.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie runs across the drawbridge and into the castle.
paragraphs.simple: He saw Annie running fast across the real drawbridge. Then she went through the gate into the castle, and he could not see her.

paragraphs.context: When he got to the bridge, he started
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack crosses the wooden bridge.
paragraphs.simple: When he got to the bridge, he started across. The wooden planks made long, high sounds under his feet.

paragraphs.context: Jack dashed across the bridge. He ran through
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack runs into the castle courtyard.
paragraphs.simple: Jack ran fast across the bridge. He ran through the castle gate and into the open space inside the walls.

paragraphs.context: Torches lit the high wall around the courtyard.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Fire torches light the walls.
paragraphs.simple: Fire torches lit the high wall around the courtyard. Almost no one was there.

paragraphs.context: Two boys led horses that clopped over the
paragraphs.mainIdea: Boys lead horses over the stone ground.
paragraphs.simple: Two boys led horses. The horses' feet made loud sounds on the round gray stones.

background.note: Long ago, many roads were made with round stones called cobblestones.

paragraphs.context: She was hiding behind a well in the
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie is hiding behind a well.
paragraphs.simple: Annie was hiding behind a well in the middle of the courtyard. She waved at him.

background.note: A well is a deep hole in the ground with water at the bottom. Castles had a well inside the walls, so people had water when enemies came.

paragraphs.context: “The feast in the Great Hall!” whispered Jack.
paragraphs.mainIdea: They see the feast in the Great Hall.
paragraphs.simple: "The feast in the Great Hall!" Jack said quietly. He stopped breathing for a moment and looked with wonder.

paragraphs.context: A giant fireplace blazed at one end of
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Great Hall is loud and full of people and food.
paragraphs.simple: A giant fire burned at one end of the noisy room. Deer horns and rugs hung on the stone walls. Flowers were on the floor. Boys in short dresses carried huge plates of food.

background.note: The boys are wearing tunics, long shirts that men and boys wore at that time. To Jack they look like short dresses.

paragraphs.context: People in bright clothes and funny hats strolled
paragraphs.mainIdea: Entertainers walk among the people and play music and tricks.
paragraphs.simple: People in bright clothes and funny hats walked slowly in the crowd. Some played guitars with funny shapes. Some threw balls in the air and caught them. Some stood swords up on their hands.

background.term: People in bright clothes and funny hats
background.note: These are jesters and jugglers. They made people laugh and did tricks at feasts. The funny-shaped guitars are lutes, an old music instrument.

paragraphs.context: Men and women dressed in capes and furs
paragraphs.mainIdea: Rich people in capes and furs sit at the long tables.
paragraphs.simple: Men and women wearing capes and furs sat at long, crowded wooden tables.

paragraphs.context: “I don’t know,” whispered Annie. “But they’re eating
paragraphs.mainIdea: People at the feast eat with their fingers.
paragraphs.simple: "I don't know," Annie said quietly. "But they're eating with their fingers."

background.note: At that time, people in Europe ate with knives and their fingers. Forks were not common yet.

paragraphs.context: “Who art thou?” he asked angrily.
paragraphs.mainIdea: A man asks them who they are, in old English.
paragraphs.simple: "Who are you?" he asked angrily.

background.note: This is old English. "Art" means "are" and "thou" means "you". So it means "Who are you?"

paragraphs.context: “Here! Quick!” Annie dashed toward a door off
paragraphs.mainIdea: They run into a dark room.
paragraphs.simple: "Here! Quick!" Annie ran to a door in the hallway and pushed it open. They both almost fell into a dark, cold room. The door closed behind them with a creak.

paragraphs.context: The light fell on shiny breastplates, leg plates,
paragraphs.mainIdea: The room is full of armor and weapons.
paragraphs.simple: The light fell on shiny metal pieces for the chest, the legs and the arms. It fell on shelves with helmets and weapons, and on shields, spears, swords, crossbows, clubs and battle-axes.

background.note: A crossbow is an old weapon. It shoots short arrows and is very strong.

paragraphs.context: He bent over and dragged the helmet over
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack puts on a heavy helmet, and it covers his face.
paragraphs.simple: He bent down and pulled the helmet over his head. The front part of the helmet fell shut with a loud noise.

paragraphs.context: Oh, forget it. It was worse than having
paragraphs.mainIdea: The helmet is much heavier than Jack thought.
paragraphs.simple: It was no good. It was worse than having a five-year-old on your head. It was more like having a ten-year-old on your head.
paragraphs.tone: This is funny: Jack uses his own idea from before to show how heavy the helmet is.

paragraphs.context: Suddenly he lost his balance and went crashing
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack falls into the armor with a big crash.
paragraphs.simple: Suddenly he could not stand straight, and he fell hard into other pieces of armor.

paragraphs.context: Someone grabbed him by the arm. The next
paragraphs.mainIdea: Someone pulls off Jack's helmet.
paragraphs.simple: Someone took his arm. Very quickly, his helmet was pulled off. He was looking into the bright light of a fire torch.

paragraphs.context: One with very squinty eyes held the torch.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Three guards hold Jack and Annie.
paragraphs.simple: One guard had eyes that were almost closed and he held the torch. One had a very red face and held Jack. One had a very long mustache and held Annie.

paragraphs.context: “Spies? Foreigners? Egyptians? Romans? Persians?” said the squinty-eyed
paragraphs.mainIdea: The guards think Jack and Annie are enemies from other countries.
paragraphs.simple: "Are you spies? Are you from another country? From Egypt? Rome? Persia?" said the guard with the small eyes.

background.note: Egypt, Rome and Persia were big, strong countries long ago. The guard thinks Jack and Annie may be enemies from far away.

paragraphs.context: The guards marched Jack and Annie out of
paragraphs.mainIdea: The guards take them out of the armory.
paragraphs.simple: The guards made Jack and Annie walk out of the armory. Jack looked back in a worried, fast way. Where was his backpack?

paragraphs.context: The fiery torch lit the dungeon. There were
paragraphs.mainIdea: The dungeon is dark, wet and dirty.
paragraphs.simple: The fire torch lit the dungeon. Chains hung from the very dirty walls. Water fell from the ceiling and made little pools on the stone floor. It was the scariest place Jack had ever seen.

background.note: A dungeon is a dark prison under a castle. In old times, people were kept there in chains.

paragraphs.context: “We’ll keep them here till the feast is
paragraphs.mainIdea: The guards want to give them to the Duke.
paragraphs.simple: "We will keep them here until the feast is over. Then we will give them to the Duke," said Squinty. "He knows how to punish thieves."
paragraphs.tone: The guard says "take care of", which sounds kind, but he means "punish". It is a scary joke.

background.note: A duke was a very important man, just below a king. He owned the castle and the land around it.

paragraphs.context: The guards started toward them. Annie whipped her
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie takes out her flashlight.
paragraphs.simple: The guards started to walk toward them. Annie took her flashlight out of the pack very fast.

paragraphs.context: Annie switched the light on. The guards gasped
paragraphs.mainIdea: The guards are afraid of the flashlight.
paragraphs.simple: Annie switched the light on. The guards breathed in fast with fear and jumped back against the wall.
paragraphs.tone: The guards have never seen a flashlight, so they think it is magic.

paragraphs.context: Squinty dropped the torch. It fell into a
paragraphs.mainIdea: The guard drops his torch and it goes out.
paragraphs.simple: Squinty dropped the torch. It fell into a dirty pool of water on the floor, made a few small sounds and stopped burning.

paragraphs.context: Annie fiercely pointed her light at one, then
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie points her light at the guards, and they are afraid.
paragraphs.simple: Annie pointed her light at one guard, then at the other, in a strong, angry way. Each one cried out and covered his face.

paragraphs.context: Jack pushed the door shut. Then Annie shined
paragraphs.mainIdea: They hide in a room with sacks and barrels.
paragraphs.simple: Jack closed the door. Then Annie shone her flashlight around the room. There were rows of big bags and wooden barrels.

paragraphs.context: Jack held his breath. A light from a
paragraphs.mainIdea: A guard looks into the room with a torch.
paragraphs.simple: Jack stopped breathing. The light from a torch moved quickly over the bags and barrels.

paragraphs.context: “Here’s a map of the castle,” he said.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The book has a map of the castle.
paragraphs.simple: "Here's a map of the castle," he said. "Look, this must be our room. It's a room for food and other things." Jack studied the room in the book. "These are bags of flour and barrels of wine."

paragraphs.context: This door leads from the storeroom through a
paragraphs.mainIdea: The book tells about a secret way out.
paragraphs.simple: This door leads from the storeroom through a secret tunnel to a high, steep place over the moat.

paragraphs.context: He put the flashlight on the floor. He
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack tries to lift the stone.
paragraphs.simple: He put the flashlight on the floor. He pushed his fingers under the thin, flat stone and tried to lift it.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie tugged on the rope handle
paragraphs.mainIdea: They open the small door in the floor.
paragraphs.simple: Jack and Annie pulled hard on the rope handle of the door. The door fell open with a low, heavy sound.

paragraphs.context: He crouched down and began moving through the
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack moves through the dark, wet tunnel.
paragraphs.simple: He bent down low and started to move through the wet, scary tunnel. The flashlight almost did not light the stone walls.

paragraphs.context: He was desperate to get out of the
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack wants to get out before the light dies.
paragraphs.simple: He wanted very much to get out of the castle before the batteries stopped working.

paragraphs.context: Jack inched down, bit by bit. Until he
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack hangs from the edge of the door.
paragraphs.simple: Jack moved down slowly, a little at a time, until he was hanging out of the door and holding on to the narrow edge.

paragraphs.context: Water filled Jack’s nose and covered his head.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack falls into the cold water of the moat.
paragraphs.simple: Water went into Jack's nose and covered his head. His glasses fell off, but he caught them just in time. He coughed and moved his arms wildly.

paragraphs.context: “I’m in … the moat!” said Jack, gasping
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack is in the moat and can hardly stay up.
paragraphs.simple: "I'm in ... the moat!" said Jack. He was trying hard to breathe. He tried to stay up by moving his legs and to put his glasses on again. His backpack, shoes and heavy clothes pulled him down.

paragraphs.context: He heard Annie swimming, too. At first it
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack hears a splash behind him.
paragraphs.simple: He heard Annie swimming too. First he thought she was swimming in front of him. But then he heard a splash behind him.

paragraphs.context: Jack’s heart almost stopped. Crocodiles? He couldn’t see
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack is afraid there are crocodiles.
paragraphs.simple: Jack was so afraid that his heart almost stopped. Crocodiles? He could not see anything through his wet glasses.

paragraphs.context: Jack swam through the dark toward her voice.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack imagines a crocodile after him.
paragraphs.simple: Jack swam through the dark toward her voice. He imagined a crocodile moving after him like a snake.

paragraphs.context: Jack grabbed her hand. She pulled him to
paragraphs.mainIdea: They climb out of the moat.
paragraphs.simple: Jack took her hand. She pulled him to the side of the moat. They climbed over a wall of earth onto the wet grass.

paragraphs.context: He was shivering all over. His teeth were
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack is very cold.
paragraphs.simple: He was shaking all over. His teeth were knocking together. He shook the water off his glasses and put them on again.

paragraphs.context: Everything had been swallowed up by the thick,
paragraphs.mainIdea: The thick darkness hides everything.
paragraphs.simple: The thick, heavy darkness covered everything, so they could not see anything.

paragraphs.context: Just then the clouds parted. A full moon
paragraphs.mainIdea: The moon comes out.
paragraphs.simple: Just then the clouds moved apart. A full moon was shining in the sky. A round area of light spread through the mist.

paragraphs.context: He sat on the black horse. His armor
paragraphs.mainIdea: The knight on his black horse is looking at them.
paragraphs.simple: He sat on the black horse. His armor shone in the moonlight. The front of his helmet hid his face. But he seemed to be looking straight at Jack and Annie.

paragraphs.context: The knight got on behind them. He slapped
paragraphs.mainIdea: The knight starts the horse.
paragraphs.simple: The knight got on behind them. He hit the horse lightly with the reins, so it started to go.

paragraphs.context: The black horse cantered beside the moonlit water
paragraphs.mainIdea: The horse runs beside the moat in the moonlight.
paragraphs.simple: The black horse ran quite fast next to the moat. The water was bright in the moonlight.

paragraphs.context: Jack rocked back and forth in the saddle.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack feels brave and strong on the horse.
paragraphs.simple: Jack moved forward and back in the saddle. The wind blew his hair. He felt very brave and very strong.

paragraphs.context: He felt as if he could ride forever
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack wishes the ride would never end.
paragraphs.simple: He felt that he could ride on this horse with this strange knight forever: over the ocean, over the world, over the moon.
paragraphs.tone: "Over the moon" is also an English idiom. It means "very, very happy". Jack is really over the moon here!

paragraphs.context: Clouds started to cover the moon again. For
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack sees the knight one last time.
paragraphs.simple: Clouds started to cover the moon again. For a short moment, Jack thought he saw the knight's armor shining on top of a hill behind the castle.

paragraphs.context: Jack heard Annie fumble in the darkness. He
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie looks for the book in the dark.
paragraphs.simple: Jack heard Annie moving her hands around clumsily in the dark. He kept looking out of the window.

paragraphs.context: “Okay. I’m going to use this,” said Annie.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie makes the wish to go home.
paragraphs.simple: "OK. I'm going to use this book," said Annie, "because I think it's the right one. Let's try. OK. I'm pointing. I'm going to wish. I wish we could go to Frog Creek!"

paragraphs.context: “Wait.” In a daze, Jack unzipped his backpack.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack puts the wet castle book back.
paragraphs.simple: "Wait." Not thinking clearly, Jack opened his backpack. He took out the castle book. It was very wet. But Jack put it back with all the other books.

paragraphs.context: Their house was so different from the dark,
paragraphs.mainIdea: Home feels safe and warm after the castle.
paragraphs.simple: Their house was so different from the dark, cold castle. It was safe and warm and friendly.

paragraphs.context: Jack held the bookmark close to his lamp
paragraphs.mainIdea: The bookmark looks very old.
paragraphs.simple: Jack held the bookmark near his lamp and studied it. The leather was smooth and thin from use. It looked very old.

paragraphs.context: The person who had dropped the gold medallion
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack understands: the same person owns the medallion and the books.
paragraphs.simple: The person who lost the gold medallion in the time of the dinosaurs was the same person who owned all the books in the tree house.

paragraphs.context: He dreamed they were with the knight again.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack dreams about the knight.
paragraphs.simple: He dreamed that they were with the knight again. All three of them were riding the black horse through the cool, dark night, past the outer wall of the castle and up over a hill in the moonlight.

paragraphs.context: Maybe M wanted the gold medallion back. The one Jack had found
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack thinks M may want the medallion and the bookmark back.
paragraphs.simple: Jack thinks about two things from their past trips: a gold medallion from the dinosaur trip and a leather bookmark from the castle trip. Maybe M wants them back.

background.note: Jack found this round gold thing with an M on it in Book 1, in the time of dinosaurs.
Jack found this in Book 2, in the castle book. It also has an M on it.

paragraphs.context: Jack silently thanked the Pteranodon who had saved him from a Tyrannosaurus
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack remembers the Pteranodon that saved him.
paragraphs.simple: In Book 1, a big flying animal called a Pteranodon saved Jack from a big meat-eating dinosaur, the Tyrannosaurus rex.

background.note: A large flying animal from the time of dinosaurs, about 80 million years ago. It was not a bird.
One of the biggest meat-eating dinosaurs. People often call it "T. rex".

paragraphs.context: She held up a book about ancient Egypt.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie finds a book about ancient Egypt.
paragraphs.simple: Annie holds up a book about Egypt long ago.

background.note: Egypt is a country in Africa. About 3,000 to 5,000 years ago it had kings called pharaohs, and they built the pyramids.

paragraphs.context: Going toward the pyramid was a long parade. Four huge cows with
paragraphs.mainIdea: The picture shows a funeral going to a pyramid.
paragraphs.simple: The picture shows a long line of people walking to a pyramid. Four big cows pull a long gold box on a sled. At the end there is a black cat.

background.note: The pyramids of Egypt are huge stone buildings with four sides that meet at the top. Kings and queens were put in them after they died.
In ancient Egypt, people loved cats. They thought cats were special, and some cats were even made into mummies.

paragraphs.context: It was true. Pyramids were high on his list of favorite things
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack likes pyramids a lot, but knights more.
paragraphs.simple: Jack loves pyramids. He likes knights best, then pyramids, and dinosaurs last.
paragraphs.tone: A small joke. After meeting a T. rex, Jack now likes dinosaurs much less. A pyramid cannot eat him, so it is safer.

paragraphs.context: Annie found the book with the picture of their hometown in it
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie finds the book about their home town.
paragraphs.simple: Annie finds the Pennsylvania book. It always takes them home.

background.note: Frog Creek is the made-up home town of Jack and Annie. Pennsylvania is a state in the east of the USA.

paragraphs.context: When a royal person died, a grand funeral procession took place. Family
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack reads about Egyptian funerals.
paragraphs.simple: When a king or queen died, there was a big, slow walk to the tomb. Family, servants and sad people walked behind the coffin. The coffin was called a sarcophagus. Four oxen pulled it on a sled.

background.note: A big stone coffin. Egyptians put the mummy inside a wooden coffin, and then put that coffin inside a stone sarcophagus.

background.term: pulled on a sled by four oxen
background.note: The Egyptians had no cars. Strong animals pulled heavy things on sleds over the sand.

paragraphs.context: “Oh, man,” said Jack weakly. “Mummies!” She sure knew how to get
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie gets Jack to come by shouting "Mummies!"
paragraphs.simple: Jack says "Oh, man" weakly. Annie knows that Jack loves mummies, so she shouts the word to make him come.
paragraphs.tone: Annie is clever with her brother. "She sure knew how to get to him" means she knows what makes Jack want to go.

paragraphs.context: “Mirage. It happens in the desert all the time,” said Jack. “It
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack says the parade was a mirage.
paragraphs.simple: Jack says a mirage is something you seem to see in a hot desert, but it is not really there. Hot air bends the sunlight.

background.note: In a hot desert, hot air near the ground bends light. So people seem to see water or things far away that are not really there.

paragraphs.context: Pyramids were sometimes called Houses of the Dead. They were nearly all
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack reads about the inside of pyramids.
paragraphs.simple: People called pyramids Houses of the Dead. They were almost all stone, but deep inside there were rooms for the dead king or queen.

background.note: The pyramids were tombs. Egyptians built them to keep the bodies of their kings and queens safe forever.
The rooms deep inside a pyramid where the mummy and its treasure were kept.

paragraphs.context: It was a gold stick. About a foot long. A dog’s
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie finds a gold stick with a dog's head.
paragraphs.simple: The thing is a gold stick, about 30 cm long, with a dog's head carved on one end.

background.note: Many Egyptian gods had animal heads. Anubis, the god of the dead, had the head of a dog-like animal (a jackal).

paragraphs.context: “It’s a thing kings and queens carry,” said Jack. “It means
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack explains what a scepter is.
paragraphs.simple: Jack says kings and queens carry a scepter to show their power.

background.term: a thing kings and queens carry
background.note: A scepter is a special stick. In many countries, kings and queens held one to show they were the rulers.

paragraphs.context: Tomb robbers often carried off the treasure buried with mummies. False passages
paragraphs.mainIdea: The book tells about tomb robbers.
paragraphs.simple: Robbers often took the gold that was put in tombs with mummies. Sometimes false ways inside the pyramids were built to stop them.

background.note: Egyptians put gold and other costly things in tombs. So robbers broke into many pyramids and took the treasure.
Builders made hallways that went nowhere, to trick robbers and keep the treasure safe.

paragraphs.context: She wore flowers in her black hair. Her long white dress had
paragraphs.mainIdea: The lady wears Egyptian clothes and gold.
paragraphs.simple: The lady has flowers in her black hair, a long white dress with many small folds, and shining gold jewelry.

background.note: Rich Egyptian women often wore thin white dresses with many small folds. Egypt is hot, so light white cloth was good.

paragraphs.context: “I am Hutepi,” she said. “Queen of the Nile. Is it true
paragraphs.mainIdea: The ghost says she is Queen Hutepi.
paragraphs.simple: The ghost says her name is Hutepi, Queen of the Nile. She asks if they have come to help her.

background.note: The Nile is the great river of Egypt. Almost all Egyptians lived near it, so "Queen of the Nile" means queen of Egypt.

paragraphs.context: “Someone must find my Book of the Dead,” she said. “I need
paragraphs.mainIdea: The queen needs her Book of the Dead to go on to the Next Life.
paragraphs.simple: The queen says someone must find her Book of the Dead. She needs it to go on to the Next Life.

background.note: A long paper with magic words and pictures. Egyptians put it in the tomb to help the dead person on the way to the next life.
Ancient Egyptians believed that people live again after death, in another world. So they put food, gold and things in tombs to use there.

paragraphs.context: “It will tell me the magic spells I need to get through
paragraphs.mainIdea: The book will tell her the magic words for the Underworld.
paragraphs.simple: The queen says the book has the magic words she needs to get safely through the world of the dead.

background.note: In Egyptian stories, the dead had to travel through a dangerous world under the ground before they reached the next life.

paragraphs.context: “Poisonous snakes,” said the ghost-queen. “Lakes of fire. Monsters. Demons.”
paragraphs.mainIdea: The queen tells about the horrors.
paragraphs.simple: In the Underworld there are poisonous snakes, lakes of fire, monsters and bad spirits.

background.note: In the Book of the Dead there are pictures of dangerous lakes of fire. The magic words help the dead get past them.

paragraphs.context: The ghost-queen smiled sadly. “Alas, my brother forgot my strange problem
paragraphs.mainIdea: The queen cannot read things close to her eyes.
paragraphs.simple: The queen says sadly that her brother forgot her problem: she cannot see things that are near her eyes. So she could not read his message for a thousand years.
paragraphs.tone: The queen speaks in an old, polite way: "Alas" (sadly), "that which" (what). Annie answers in a very simple way: Jack has the same problem and wears glasses. This is a little joke.

paragraphs.context: “Hieroglyphs!” said Jack, finally finding his voice. “It’s the ancient Egyptian
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack explains hieroglyphs.
paragraphs.simple: Jack says hieroglyphs are the old Egyptian way of writing with pictures.

background.note: About 700 small pictures. Some stood for things, some for sounds. Chinese characters also began as pictures long ago.

paragraphs.context: “Maybe it’s supposed to carry her to the Next Life,” said
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack thinks the boat will carry the queen to the Next Life.
paragraphs.simple: Jack thinks the boat is there to take the queen to the Next Life.

background.term: carry her to the Next Life
background.note: Egyptians thought the dead traveled by boat, like the sun god who sailed across the sky in a boat. Real boats were found next to the pyramids.

paragraphs.context: The boat was filled with many things. Gold plates. Painted cups. Jeweled
paragraphs.mainIdea: The boat is full of beautiful things.
paragraphs.simple: In the boat there are gold plates, painted cups, cups with jewels, baskets, blue jewelry and small wooden statues.

background.note: Egyptians put small figures of servants in tombs. They believed the figures would work for the dead person in the next life.

paragraphs.context: Jack reached into the jug and pulled out the folded cloth. It
paragraphs.mainIdea: Inside the cloth there is a scroll.
paragraphs.simple: Jack takes the folded cloth out of the jug. An old scroll is inside it.

background.note: Egyptians wrote on paper made from a water plant called papyrus. They rolled long papers into scrolls.

paragraphs.context: Her broken teeth were showing. Her little wrinkled ears. Her squashed nose
paragraphs.mainIdea: The mummy is old and broken.
paragraphs.simple: The mummy has broken teeth, small wrinkled ears, a flat nose, dry skin and empty holes for eyes.
paragraphs.tone: The writer uses many short parts, like a list. It feels like we are looking at the face one part at a time with Jack.

paragraphs.context: Ancient Egyptians tried to protect the body so it would last forever
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack reads how Egyptians made a mummy.
paragraphs.simple: Egyptians tried to keep the body safe forever. First they dried it with salt.

background.note: Egyptians used a special salt called natron. It took about 40 days to dry the body.

paragraphs.context: Next it was covered with oil. Then it was wrapped tightly in
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack reads more about making a mummy.
paragraphs.simple: Next the body got oil on it, then it was wrapped tightly in long cloths. The brain was taken out.
paragraphs.tone: The sentence stops at "by—" because Annie cries "Stop!" It is a funny break: she does not want to hear the gross part.

background.note: The body was wrapped in hundreds of metres of long, thin cloth.

paragraphs.context: “I hope it’s peanut butter and jelly sandwiches,” he said.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack hopes for peanut butter and jelly sandwiches.
paragraphs.simple: Jack hopes Mom is making his favorite lunch.

background.note: A very common American lunch for children: bread with peanut butter and sweet fruit jam ("jelly" in American English).

paragraphs.context: “A talking parrot!” said Annie. “Is your name Polly? Can I call
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie wants to call the parrot Polly.
paragraphs.simple: Annie is happy to see a talking parrot. She asks if its name is Polly.

background.note: In English, Polly is a very common name for a pet parrot. Many parrots learn to say "Polly wants a cracker".

paragraphs.context: The flag was black. With a skull and crossbones.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The ship has a pirate flag.
paragraphs.simple: The flag is black, with a skull and two bones under it.

background.note: This picture means danger or death. Pirates put it on their flags to make other ships afraid.

paragraphs.context: “Pirates of the Caribbean,” Jack read aloud.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The book is about pirates of the Caribbean.
paragraphs.simple: Jack reads the title out loud: Pirates of the Caribbean.

background.note: The Caribbean Sea has many islands. About 300 years ago, many pirates attacked ships there.

paragraphs.context: “Pirates?” squeaked Annie. “Like in Peter Pan?”
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie thinks of Peter Pan.
paragraphs.simple: Annie asks if the pirates are like the ones in Peter Pan.

background.note: A famous story about a boy who never grows up. In it there are pirates and a bad pirate leader, Captain Hook.

paragraphs.context: Three hundred years ago, pirates raided Spanish treasure ships in the Caribbean
paragraphs.mainIdea: The book tells about pirates long ago.
paragraphs.simple: About 300 years ago, pirates attacked Spanish ships with treasure in the Caribbean Sea.

background.note: At that time Spain had many lands in America. Its ships carried gold and silver from there back to Spain, so pirates attacked them.

paragraphs.context: The skull-and-crossbones flag was called the Jolly Roger.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The pirate flag has a name.
paragraphs.simple: The black flag with a skull and bones was called the Jolly Roger.

background.note: The name of the pirate flag. No one is sure where the name came from.

paragraphs.context: “No one escapes Cap’n Bones!” he roared. His breath was terrible.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The big pirate says his name is Cap’n Bones.
paragraphs.simple: The pirate shouts that no one gets away from Captain Bones.

background.note: "Cap’n" is pirate talk for "captain". "Bones" is a scary name for a pirate.

paragraphs.context: “Aye, aye, Cap’n!” they answered. And they started up the ladder
paragraphs.mainIdea: The pirates answer their captain.
paragraphs.simple: The two pirates say "Yes, sir!" and climb up to the tree house.

background.note: Sailors say "Aye, aye" to their captain. It means "Yes, I will do it."

paragraphs.context: “Another book!” roared Cap’n Bones. “That’s vile booty!”
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cap’n Bones hates books.
paragraphs.simple: Cap’n Bones shouts that a book is horrible treasure.
paragraphs.tone: Pirates think only gold is good. Books are "vile booty" (bad treasure) to him. This is the opposite of what Jack and Morgan believe.

paragraphs.context: “Aye, it’s the map telling about Kidd’s treasure.”
paragraphs.mainIdea: Bones has a map of Kidd’s treasure.
paragraphs.simple: Cap’n Bones says the map tells where Captain Kidd's treasure is.

background.note: Captain William Kidd was a real pirate (about 1645-1701). People still tell stories that he buried treasure on an island.

paragraphs.context: “Which kid’s treasure? Not us kids,” said Annie. “We don’t
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie thinks "Kidd" means "kid".
paragraphs.simple: Annie thinks he is talking about a child's treasure, not Captain Kidd's treasure.
paragraphs.tone: A word joke: "Kidd" (the name) and "kid" (a child) sound the same.

paragraphs.context: “You know he can’t read,” said Stinky.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The pirates say Bones cannot read.
paragraphs.simple: Stinky tells Jack that Cap’n Bones cannot read.

background.note: Long ago, many sailors never went to school, so a lot of them could not read.

paragraphs.context: “Okay,” said Jack. “I’ll read it to you.” He looked at
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack reads the map.
paragraphs.simple: Jack reads the words on the map: "The gold is under the whale's eye."

background.note: Old English. "Doth" means "does". So "the gold doth lie beneath" means "the gold lies under".

paragraphs.context: The air was filled with wild fiddle music and bagpipes playing. And
paragraphs.mainIdea: The ship is wild and noisy.
paragraphs.simple: On the ship there is wild music, and pirates shouting and laughing in an ugly way.

background.note: A fiddle is a violin. Bagpipes are a loud music instrument from Scotland. Sailors played music for fun on long trips.

paragraphs.context: Captain Kidd was a famous pirate. It is said that he buried
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack and Annie read about Captain Kidd.
paragraphs.simple: Captain Kidd was a famous pirate. People say he buried a box of gold and jewels on an island with no people.

background.note: A real Scottish sailor and pirate, about 300 years ago. Some people still look for his treasure today.

paragraphs.context: “A whale. A huge whale. As big as a football field.”
paragraphs.mainIdea: The whale is very big.
paragraphs.simple: Annie says the whale is as big as a football field.

background.note: An American football field is about 110 metres long.

paragraphs.context: “The bird’s an omen, Cap’n!” shouted Stinky.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Stinky thinks the parrot is a bad sign.
paragraphs.simple: Stinky shouts that the bird is a sign of bad luck.

background.note: Sailors long ago believed in many signs of good and bad luck, like birds or the weather.

paragraphs.context: “Mutineers! Come back!” shouted Cap’n Bones. He dragged Jack and Annie
paragraphs.mainIdea: The pirates run away from their captain.
paragraphs.simple: Cap’n Bones shouts that his men are mutineers. He runs after them with Jack and Annie.

background.note: On a ship, the captain's word was law. Sailors who would not do what the captain said were mutineers, and they could be killed.

paragraphs.context: Then, in a great swirl of colors—in a blur of feathers
paragraphs.mainIdea: Polly changes into a woman.
paragraphs.simple: In a turning cloud of colors, feathers and light, a new person slowly appears.
paragraphs.tone: The long sentence with many "in a ..." parts feels fast and magic, like the change itself.

paragraphs.context: “Hello, Jack. Hello, Annie,” the old woman said. “My name is Morgan
paragraphs.mainIdea: The old woman says her name.
paragraphs.simple: The old woman says hello. Her name is Morgan le Fay.

background.note: In old English stories about King Arthur, Morgan le Fay is a woman who can do magic. Here she is kind.

paragraphs.context: “Have you ever heard of King Arthur?” said Morgan.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Morgan asks about King Arthur.
paragraphs.simple: Morgan asks if Jack knows about King Arthur.

background.note: A famous king in old British stories. He and his knights met at a Round Table.

paragraphs.context: “You’re from Camelot,” said Jack. “I’ve read about Camelot.”
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack knows about Camelot.
paragraphs.simple: Jack says Morgan comes from Camelot. He has read about it.

background.note: The castle and town of King Arthur in the old stories.

paragraphs.context: “You—you’re a witch.”
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack has read that Morgan is a witch.
paragraphs.simple: Jack says that in his books, Morgan le Fay is a witch.

background.note: In many King Arthur stories Morgan is a bad witch. Here she says: "You can’t believe everything you read."

paragraphs.context: “Yes. And I’ve come to the 20th century, your time, to
paragraphs.mainIdea: Morgan collects books from Jack's time.
paragraphs.simple: Morgan says she came to Jack's time to get books. Jack and Annie are lucky to live in a time with so many books.

background.note: The years 1901 to 2000. The book came out in 1994.

paragraphs.context: “Oh yes. Many wonderful books. I want to borrow them for our
paragraphs.mainIdea: Morgan wants books for her scribes to copy.
paragraphs.simple: Morgan wants to borrow the books so her writers can copy them by hand.

background.note: In King Arthur's time there were no machines to print books. Scribes copied every book by hand.

paragraphs.context: “And the cat and the knight and Polly!” said Annie.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Morgan was all the animals and the knight.
paragraphs.simple: Annie understands that Morgan was the cat, the knight and Polly too.
paragraphs.tone: A surprise! Now we know who helped Jack and Annie in all four books.

paragraphs.context: “Never,” said Morgan. She smiled at both of them. “You remind me
paragraphs.mainIdea: Morgan says what she likes in Jack and Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Morgan says they are like her. Annie loves impossible things, and Jack loves knowledge. That is the best mix.
paragraphs.tone: Warm and kind. Morgan says the two children are different, and that together they are best.

paragraphs.context: They had treasure at home. A ton of it. Everywhere.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack sees that home is full of treasure.
paragraphs.simple: Jack thinks they do not need the treasure chest. There is treasure everywhere at home.
paragraphs.tone: The end of the four books. The "treasure" is the shining world around them, not gold. Jack now thinks like Annie.

sentences.context: This is what he got for spending time with his seven-year-old sister
sentences.simple: This is what happens when you spend time with a little sister of seven.
sentences.main: This is what he got.

parts.meaning: This was the result for Jack

parts.text: for spending time with his seven-year-old sister
parts.meaning: because he spent time with his sister, who was seven.

sentences.grammar: Jack is not happy. "This is what you get for ..." means "this bad thing happens because you ...". "Seven-year-old" joins four words to say how old she is.

sentences.context: He was about to call again when Annie poked her head out of the tree house window
sentences.simple: Jack was going to call her again. Just then Annie put her head out of the window.
sentences.main: He was about to call again.

parts.text: He was about to call again
parts.job: What Jack was going to do.
parts.meaning: Jack was just going to call again,

parts.text: when Annie poked her head out of the tree house window
parts.meaning: but at that moment Annie put her head out of the window.

sentences.grammar: "Was about to ... when ..." means one thing was going to happen, but something else happened first.

sentences.context: But even as he said this, Jack opened the dinosaur book to where the bookmark was
sentences.simple: At the same time as he said "No", Jack opened the dinosaur book at the page with the bookmark.
sentences.main: Jack opened the dinosaur book.

parts.text: But even as he said this
parts.job: When. "Even as" means "at the very same time as".
parts.meaning: But while he was saying this,
Jack opened the dinosaur book
at the page with the bookmark.

sentences.grammar: Find the main part after the comma. "Even as he said this" shows that Jack says "no" but does "yes" at the same moment.

sentences.context: Jack nearly fell out the window trying to see it
sentences.simple: Jack wanted to see the animal so much that he almost fell out of the window.
sentences.main: Jack nearly fell out the window.

parts.text: Jack nearly fell out the window
parts.meaning: Jack almost fell out of the window

parts.job: What he was doing at that time.
parts.meaning: because he was trying to see the Pteranodon.

sentences.grammar: "Nearly fell" means he did not really fall. The "trying ..." part tells you what he was doing when it almost happened.

sentences.context: The world outside and the world in the picture—they were exactly the same
sentences.simple: The real world outside the window looked just like the world in the picture.
sentences.main: They were exactly the same.

parts.text: The world outside and the world in the picture
parts.meaning: What Jack saw out of the window and what he saw in the book

parts.job: What is true about them. "They" means the two worlds.
parts.meaning: were just the same.

sentences.grammar: The writer names the two things first, then the long line (—) stops you, and "they" says them again. This makes the surprise bigger.

sentences.context: They couldn’t have landed in a time 65 million years ago
sentences.simple: It was not possible that they were now in a time 65 million years ago.
sentences.main: They couldn't have landed there.

parts.job: Main part. "Couldn't have" means "it is not possible that they did".
parts.meaning: It is not possible that they arrived

parts.text: in a time 65 million years ago
parts.meaning: in a time 65 million years in the past.

sentences.grammar: "Couldn't have + done" is what you say when you think something in the past is impossible. Jack does not want to believe it.

sentences.context: “He’s no dog, Annie.”
sentences.simple: He is not a dog, Annie. Don't think about him like that.
sentences.main: He's no dog.

parts.meaning: He is not a dog at all, Annie.

sentences.grammar: "He's no dog" is stronger than "He's not a dog". It means "Don't think he is like a dog." Later Annie says the same to Jack: "She's no dog, Jack."

sentences.context: We’re probably the first people in the whole world to ever see a real live Pteranodon
sentences.simple: We are maybe the first people ever who have seen a real, living Pteranodon.
sentences.main: We're probably the first people.

parts.text: We’re probably the first people in the whole world
parts.meaning: We are maybe the first people of all

parts.text: to ever see a real live Pteranodon
parts.job: The first people to do what.
parts.meaning: who have ever seen a living Pteranodon.

sentences.grammar: "The first people to see" means "the first people who saw". "Live" here sounds like "five" and means "alive".

sentences.context: His brain’s probably no bigger than a bean
sentences.simple: His brain is maybe only as big as a bean.
sentences.main: His brain is very small.

parts.meaning: His brain is

parts.text: probably no bigger than a bean
parts.meaning: maybe not bigger than a bean.

sentences.grammar: "No bigger than" means "as small as". Jack thinks the animal is not smart. "Brain's" is short for "brain is", not "of the brain".

sentences.context: You can’t just go running to a nest of babies
sentences.simple: You should not run to a nest of babies without thinking.
sentences.main: You can't go running to a nest.

parts.job: Main part. "Can't just" means "you should not, without thinking".
parts.meaning: You should not simply

parts.text: go running to a nest of babies
parts.meaning: run to a nest with babies in it.

sentences.grammar: Here "can't" is not about being able. It means "it is not a good idea". "Go running" means "run".

sentences.context: While a few mothers baby-sat the nests, others hunted for food
sentences.simple: Some mothers watched the nests. At the same time, the other mothers looked for food.
sentences.main: Others hunted for food.

parts.text: While a few mothers baby-sat the nests
parts.job: At the same time. "While" means "during the time that".
parts.meaning: When a few mothers watched the nests
the other mothers looked for food.

sentences.grammar: "While ..." tells you two things happen at the same time. "Baby-sat" is the past of "baby-sit": to look after babies.

sentences.context: What he saw in the distance almost made him throw up
sentences.simple: He saw something far away. It was so scary that he almost felt sick.
sentences.main: What he saw almost made him throw up.

parts.text: What he saw in the distance
parts.job: Who or what did it: the thing he saw.
parts.meaning: The thing that Jack saw far away
almost made him sick.

sentences.grammar: The first part, "What he saw in the distance", is one long name for a thing. Ask: what made him sick? The thing he saw. The writer does not tell you what it is until the next lines.

sentences.context: Did fear of the Tyrannosaurus send them home
sentences.simple: Did the mothers come back to their nests because they were afraid of the Tyrannosaurus?
sentences.main: Did fear send them home?

parts.meaning: Was it because they were afraid of the T. rex
that they came back home?

sentences.grammar: Here "fear" is like a person who does something: fear "sends" them home. It means they went home because they were afraid.

sentences.context: His heart was beating so fast he could hardly think
sentences.simple: His heart beat very fast, and he almost could not think.
sentences.main: His heart was beating fast.

parts.text: His heart was beating so fast
parts.meaning: His heart was beating very, very fast,

parts.job: What happened because of it. "Hardly" means "almost not".
parts.meaning: so he almost could not think.

sentences.grammar: "So fast (that) he could hardly think": "so ... (that)" tells you the result. The word "that" is often left out. "Hardly" does not mean "hard".

sentences.context: If it were alive today, it would eat a human in one bite
sentences.simple: It is not alive now. But if it were, it could eat a person in one bite.
sentences.main: It would eat a human.

parts.job: An idea that is not true now.
parts.meaning: If the T. rex lived now

parts.text: it would eat a human in one bite
parts.meaning: it would eat a person in one bite.

sentences.grammar: "If it were ..., it would ..." talks about something that is not real. The T. rex is not alive, so this is only an idea. "Were" is used here even after "it".

sentences.context: Then the Pteranodon soared out over the plain—over the Triceratops who was grazing in the high grass
sentences.simple: Then the Pteranodon flew high over the flat land and over the Triceratops, which was eating grass.
sentences.main: The Pteranodon soared out over the plain.

parts.text: Then the Pteranodon soared out over the plain
parts.meaning: Then the Pteranodon flew high over the flat land,

parts.job: More about where. The long line (—) adds it.
parts.meaning: and over the Triceratops

parts.text: who was grazing in the high grass
parts.meaning: that was eating the tall grass.

sentences.grammar: The long line (—) adds more about where they flew. "Who" here is about an animal, not a person. The writer thinks of the dinosaur like a friend.

sentences.context: He grabbed it and tore through it, looking for the photograph of the Frog Creek woods
sentences.simple: He took the book and turned the pages very fast. He was looking for the photo of the Frog Creek woods.
sentences.main: He grabbed it and tore through it.

parts.job: First action. "It" is the Pennsylvania book.
parts.meaning: He took the book quickly
and turned the pages very fast,

parts.text: looking for the photograph of the Frog Creek woods
parts.meaning: because he was looking for the photo of the woods.

sentences.grammar: "Tore through" here does not mean he broke the book. It means he looked through it very fast. The "looking for ..." part tells you what he wanted.

sentences.context: No time had passed since they’d left
sentences.simple: It was the same time as when they left. The trip took no time at home.
sentences.main: No time had passed.

parts.job: Main part. "No time" is the one that "had passed".
parts.meaning: Not even one minute went by
from the moment they left.

sentences.grammar: "Had passed" and "had left" talk about a time before another time in the story. The trip was long, but at home no time went by.
