sentences.context: As they walked past all the houses on their street, the trip to dinosaur time did seem more and more like a dream
sentences.simple: When they walked past the houses on their street, the dinosaur trip began to feel more and more like a dream.
sentences.main: The trip did seem like a dream.

parts.text: As they walked past all the houses on their street
parts.meaning: While they walked past the houses on their street,

parts.job: Who or what: the main thing.
parts.meaning: the trip to the time of the dinosaurs

parts.text: did seem more and more like a dream
parts.meaning: really started to feel like a dream.

sentences.grammar: The first part ("As ...") tells you when, so find the main part after the comma. "Did seem" is stronger than "seemed": it means "really seemed".

sentences.context: What if he or she didn’t want kids to know about the tree house
sentences.simple: Maybe the magic person does not want children to know about the tree house. Jack worries about this.
sentences.main: What if he or she didn't want kids to know?

parts.meaning: Maybe, and that would be bad:

parts.text: he or she didn’t want kids to know about the tree house
parts.meaning: the person did not want children to know about the tree house.

sentences.grammar: "What if ...?" asks about a bad thing that may happen. Jack does not know if the magic person is a man or a woman, so he says "he or she".

sentences.context: It was the book that had taken them to the time of the dinosaurs
sentences.simple: This was the book that took them to the time of the dinosaurs.
sentences.main: It was the book.

parts.meaning: It was the same book

parts.text: that had taken them to the time of the dinosaurs
parts.meaning: that took them back to the dinosaurs.

sentences.grammar: "That had taken them ..." tells you which book. "Had taken" shows it happened before this moment, yesterday.

sentences.context: How could anyone forget seeing a real live Tyrannosaurus rex
sentences.simple: No one could ever forget seeing a living T. rex!
sentences.main: No one could forget it.

parts.job: A question that does not need an answer.
parts.meaning: No one could ever forget

parts.text: seeing a real live Tyrannosaurus rex
parts.meaning: that they saw a living T. rex.

sentences.grammar: This question does not want an answer. It means "Of course no one could forget!". After "forget", the "-ing" form ("seeing") means something you did before.

sentences.context: Besides, he sort of wanted to take a peek himself
sentences.simple: And also, he wanted a little to have a quick look too.
sentences.main: He wanted to take a peek.

parts.meaning: And also,
he wanted a little
to look quickly too.

sentences.grammar: "Besides" gives one more reason. The first reason: he could not leave Annie. The second reason: he wanted to see the castle too. "Himself" means "he too, not only Annie".

sentences.context: A helmet alone could weigh up to forty pounds
sentences.simple: Just the helmet could be as heavy as forty pounds, about 18 kilos.
sentences.main: A helmet could weigh forty pounds.

parts.meaning: Just the helmet, without the rest,

parts.text: could weigh up to forty pounds
parts.meaning: could be as heavy as forty pounds.

sentences.grammar: "Alone" after a thing means "only this thing". "Up to" means "as much as, but not more".

sentences.context: So it’d be like riding a horse with a five-year-old on your head
sentences.simple: So wearing a helmet is like riding a horse with a small child sitting on your head.
sentences.main: It'd be like riding a horse.

parts.meaning: So it would feel like
riding a horse

parts.text: with a five-year-old on your head
parts.meaning: with a five-year-old child on your head.

sentences.grammar: "It'd" is short for "it would" here. Jack is making a picture in his mind. "Your head" means anyone's head, not only the reader's.

sentences.context: The moat was filled with water, to help protect the castle from enemies
sentences.simple: The moat was full of water. This helped keep enemies away from the castle.
sentences.main: The moat was filled with water.

parts.text: The moat was filled with water
parts.meaning: The moat was full of water,

parts.text: to help protect the castle from enemies
parts.meaning: so it could help keep the castle safe from enemies.

sentences.grammar: "To help ..." after the comma tells you why. "Protect ... from" means keep something safe from danger.

sentences.context: Fanfares were played to announce different dishes in a feast
sentences.simple: At a feast, short, loud music was played to tell people a new kind of food was coming.
sentences.main: Fanfares were played.

parts.job: Main part. We do not know who played them; it is not important.
parts.meaning: Short pieces of loud music were played

parts.text: to announce different dishes in a feast
parts.meaning: to tell people about each new kind of food at a big meal.

sentences.grammar: "Were played" tells you what happened to the music, not who played it. "Dishes" here means kinds of food, not plates.

sentences.context: Not only could Jack not lift his head, he couldn’t see anything, either
sentences.simple: Jack could not lift his head. And also, he could not see anything.
sentences.main: Jack could not lift his head or see.

parts.text: Not only could Jack not lift his head
parts.meaning: Jack could not lift his head,
and he also could not see anything.

sentences.grammar: "Not only ... (but) ..." gives two things, and the second is even worse. When a sentence starts with "Not only", "could" comes before "Jack". Read it as "Jack could not lift his head".

sentences.context: The next thing he knew, his helmet was yanked off
sentences.simple: Very fast, before he understood what was happening, someone pulled his helmet off.
sentences.main: His helmet was yanked off.

parts.meaning: Suddenly, before Jack could think,

parts.job: Main part. We do not see who did it.
parts.meaning: someone pulled his helmet off hard.

sentences.grammar: "The next thing he knew" means things happened so fast that he did not understand them. "Was yanked off" tells you what happened to the helmet. Jack cannot see who did it.

sentences.context: We’ll keep them here till the feast is done
sentences.simple: We will keep them in the dungeon until the feast is over.
sentences.main: We'll keep them here.

parts.meaning: We will keep the children here
until the feast is finished.

sentences.grammar: "Till" is short for "until". "Is done" here means "is finished". After "till", English uses "is", not "will be", even for the future.

sentences.context: This door leads from the storeroom through a secret passage to a precipice over the moat
sentences.simple: This door goes from the storeroom through a hidden tunnel to a high, steep edge over the moat.
sentences.main: This door leads to a precipice.

parts.meaning: This door goes
from the room where food is kept,
through a hidden tunnel,

parts.text: to a precipice over the moat
parts.meaning: to a high, steep place over the moat.

sentences.grammar: Follow the way: "from" (start), "through" (the middle), "to" (the end). "Leads" here means "goes to".

sentences.context: He was desperate to get out of the castle before the batteries died completely
sentences.simple: He wanted very much to get out of the castle before the flashlight stopped working.
sentences.main: He was desperate to get out.

parts.job: Main part. "Desperate" means he wanted it very, very much.
parts.meaning: He wanted very much

parts.text: to get out of the castle
parts.meaning: to get out of the castle
before the batteries had no more power.

sentences.grammar: "Desperate to do" means wanting to do something very much. "Died" here is about batteries, not people: they stopped working.

sentences.context: Until he was hanging out the door, clinging to the ledge
sentences.simple: At last he was hanging out of the door and holding on to the narrow edge.
sentences.main: He was hanging out the door.

parts.text: Until he was hanging out the door
parts.meaning: until he was hanging outside the door,

parts.job: What he was doing at the same time.
parts.meaning: and holding tightly to the narrow edge.

sentences.grammar: This line has no main part. It goes with the line before: "Jack inched down, bit by bit, until he was hanging ...". Writers sometimes cut long sentences like this to make you feel the danger.

sentences.context: Then down he fell
sentences.simple: Then he fell down.
sentences.main: He fell.

parts.meaning: Then he fell down.

sentences.grammar: The writer puts "down" first to make the fall feel sudden and big. Read it as "Then he fell down."

sentences.context: With his backpack, his shoes, and his heavy clothes, he could hardly stay afloat
sentences.simple: His backpack, shoes and heavy clothes pulled him down, so he almost could not stay on top of the water.
sentences.main: He could hardly stay afloat.

parts.text: With his backpack, his shoes, and his heavy clothes
parts.meaning: Because he had his backpack, shoes and heavy clothes on,
he almost could not stay up in the water.

sentences.grammar: Find the main part after the comma. The "With ..." part gives the reason. "Hardly" does not mean "hard"; it means "almost not".

sentences.context: At first it seemed as if she was swimming in front of him
sentences.simple: First Jack thought that Annie was swimming in front of him.
sentences.main: It seemed she was in front of him.

parts.job: When. It shows that this changes later.
parts.meaning: In the beginning
Jack thought

parts.text: she was swimming in front of him
parts.meaning: that Annie was swimming in front of him.

sentences.grammar: "At first" tells you the idea will change: the next sentence says "But then ...". "It seemed as if" means "it looked like this, but maybe it was not true".

sentences.context: He couldn’t even see the moat, much less a crocodile
sentences.simple: He could not see the moat, so of course he could not see a crocodile.
sentences.main: He couldn't see the moat.

parts.text: He couldn’t even see the moat
parts.job: Main part. "Even" shows this is surprising.
parts.meaning: He could not see the big moat,

parts.job: A smaller thing that is even harder to see.
parts.meaning: so of course he could not see a crocodile in it.

sentences.grammar: "Not ... even A, much less B" means "not A, and surely not B". The moat is big, and he cannot see it, so he surely cannot see a crocodile.

sentences.context: He felt as if he could ride forever on this horse, with this mysterious knight
sentences.simple: He felt that he could ride this horse with this strange knight and never stop.
sentences.main: He felt as if he could ride forever.

parts.meaning: He felt that

parts.text: he could ride forever on this horse
parts.meaning: he could ride on this horse and never stop,
with this strange knight.

sentences.grammar: "Felt as if" tells you a feeling, not a real fact. The next lines ("Over the ocean. Over the world. Over the moon.") make the feeling bigger and bigger.

sentences.context: For a brief moment, Jack thought he saw the knight’s armor gleaming on the top of a hill beyond the castle
sentences.simple: For a short moment, Jack thought he saw the knight's armor shining on a hill behind the castle.
sentences.main: Jack thought he saw the knight's armor.

parts.meaning: For a very short time,

parts.text: Jack thought he saw the knight’s armor
parts.meaning: Jack thought he saw the knight's armor
shining

parts.text: on the top of a hill beyond the castle
parts.meaning: on a hill on the other side of the castle.

sentences.grammar: "Thought he saw" means he is not sure. Find the main part after the comma. "Beyond" means "on the other side of".

sentences.context: The person who had dropped the gold medallion in the time of the dinosaurs was the same person who owned all the books in the tree house
sentences.simple: The person who lost the gold medallion with the dinosaurs is the same person who owns the books in the tree house.
sentences.main: The person was the same person.

parts.job: Who. The main part starts here.
parts.meaning: The person

parts.text: who had dropped the gold medallion in the time of the dinosaurs
parts.meaning: who lost the gold medallion with the dinosaurs
was the same person

parts.text: who owned all the books in the tree house
parts.meaning: who owned the books in the tree house.

sentences.grammar: This is a long sentence, but the main part is short: "The person ... was the same person". Each "who ..." part tells you which person.

sentences.context: Pyramids were high on his list of favorite things. After knights. But before dinosaurs. Way before dinosaurs.
sentences.simple: Jack liked pyramids very much. He liked knights more, and he liked dinosaurs much less.
sentences.main: Pyramids were high on his list.

parts.text: Pyramids were high on his list of favorite things.
parts.meaning: Pyramids were one of the things Jack liked best.
Knights come first on his list.
Dinosaurs come after pyramids.

parts.job: Short extra part. "Way" makes it stronger.
parts.meaning: Dinosaurs are much lower on the list.

sentences.grammar: The writer uses very short parts with no "who did what". Join them to the first sentence: "after knights, but way before dinosaurs". "Way before" means "much before".

sentences.context: He didn’t have to worry about being eaten by a pyramid.
sentences.simple: A pyramid cannot eat him, so he does not need to be afraid of it.
sentences.main: He didn’t have to worry.

parts.meaning: He did not need to feel afraid

parts.text: about being eaten by a pyramid
parts.job: What he did not worry about.
parts.meaning: that a pyramid would eat him.

sentences.grammar: "Being eaten by" means something eats you. This is a joke: a T. rex almost ate Jack, but a pyramid cannot.

sentences.context: When a royal person died, a grand funeral procession took place.
sentences.simple: When a king or queen died, there was a big, slow walk to the tomb.
sentences.main: A funeral procession took place.

parts.meaning: When a king, queen or prince died,

parts.text: a grand funeral procession took place.
parts.meaning: a big line of people walked slowly with the body.

sentences.grammar: "When ..." at the start tells you the time. The main part comes after the comma. "Took place" means "happened".

sentences.context: The closer they got to the parade, the harder it was to see it.
sentences.simple: When they got nearer to the parade, it became more and more difficult to see.
sentences.main: It was harder to see the parade.

parts.text: The closer they got to the parade,
parts.meaning: As they came nearer to the parade,

parts.text: the harder it was to see it.
parts.job: The second change, which goes with the first.
parts.meaning: it got more difficult to see it.

sentences.grammar: Look for "the ...-er, the ...-er". It means when one thing grows, the other grows too: "The more you read, the better you read."

sentences.context: But it just turns out to be the sunlight reflecting through heat.
sentences.simple: But in the end it is only sunlight that bends in the hot air.
sentences.main: It turns out to be sunlight.

parts.text: But it just turns out to be
parts.job: Main part. "Turns out to be" = "in the end you find it is".
parts.meaning: But in the end it is only
light from the sun, bent by the hot air.

sentences.grammar: "Something turns out to be X" means you thought it was one thing, but it is really X.

sentences.context: They were nearly all solid stone, except for the burial chambers deep inside.
sentences.simple: Pyramids were almost all stone, but deep inside there were rooms for the dead.
sentences.main: They were nearly all solid stone.

parts.text: They were nearly all solid stone,
parts.meaning: Pyramids were almost all hard stone,

parts.text: except for the burial chambers deep inside.
parts.meaning: but not the rooms for the dead, deep in the middle.

sentences.grammar: "Except for ..." tells you the one part that is not like the rest.

sentences.context: Tomb robbers often carried off the treasure buried with mummies.
sentences.simple: Robbers often took away the gold that was put in tombs with mummies.
sentences.main: Tomb robbers carried off the treasure.

parts.text: Tomb robbers often carried off the treasure
parts.meaning: Robbers often took away the gold
that was put in the ground with the mummies.

sentences.grammar: "Buried with mummies" tells you which treasure: the treasure that was buried with them. "Carried off" means took away.

sentences.context: “Before I journey on to the Next Life, I must pass through the horrors of the Underworld.”
sentences.simple: Before I travel to the next life, I must go through the scary world of the dead.
sentences.main: I must pass through the Underworld.

parts.text: Before I journey on to the Next Life,
parts.meaning: Before I travel on to my new life after death,

parts.text: I must pass through the horrors of the Underworld.
parts.meaning: I have to go through the scary things in the world under the ground.

sentences.grammar: "Before ..." at the start tells you the time. The main part comes after the comma. You may know "a journey" (a trip). Here "journey on" means "travel on".

sentences.context: Then he carved this secret message on the wall, telling me how to find it.
sentences.simple: Then he cut a secret message into the wall. It tells me how to find the book.
sentences.main: He carved this secret message on the wall.

parts.text: Then he carved this secret message on the wall,
parts.meaning: Then my brother cut a secret message into the wall.

parts.text: telling me how to find it.
parts.meaning: The message tells me how to find the book.

sentences.grammar: The "-ing" part after the comma tells you more about the message. "It" is the Book of the Dead.

sentences.context: I cannot see clearly that which is close to my eyes.
sentences.simple: I cannot see things clearly when they are near my eyes.
sentences.main: I cannot see clearly.

parts.meaning: I cannot see well

parts.text: that which is close to my eyes.
parts.job: What she cannot see. "That which" = "what" (old style).
parts.meaning: the things that are near my eyes.

sentences.grammar: The queen talks in an old way. "That which" means "what" or "the things that".

sentences.context: Unless it was like a towel hanging over a bathroom rod.
sentences.simple: Maybe, if he thought of a towel hanging over a bar in the bathroom.
sentences.main: Unless it was like a towel.

parts.text: Unless it was like a towel
parts.job: The only way he could see it.
parts.meaning: Only if it looked like a towel
that hangs over a bar in the bathroom.

sentences.grammar: "Unless" means "if not". Read it with the sentence before: Jack could not see a folded cloth, only if he thought of a towel on a bar.

sentences.context: Or did a deep sigh seem to shudder throughout the room?
sentences.simple: Or did it feel like a long sad breath went through the whole room?
sentences.main: Did a deep sigh shudder through the room?

parts.meaning: Or did a long breath out

parts.text: seem to shudder throughout the room?
parts.meaning: seem to shake through all of the room?

sentences.grammar: Jack is not sure what happened, so he asks questions. "Seem to" means it looked or felt like that, but maybe it was not real.

sentences.context: Tucked between two branches was the tree house.
sentences.simple: The tree house was there, between two branches.
sentences.main: The tree house was tucked between two branches.

parts.meaning: Fitted safely between two branches
was the tree house.

sentences.grammar: The order is turned around. Normal order: "The tree house was tucked between two branches." Writers do this to show the place first.

sentences.context: Sitting on a branch outside the window ledge of the tree house was a green parrot.
sentences.simple: A green parrot was sitting on a branch outside the tree house window.
sentences.main: A green parrot was sitting on a branch.

parts.meaning: sitting on a branch

parts.text: outside the window ledge of the tree house
parts.meaning: just outside the tree house window
was a green parrot.

sentences.grammar: The order is turned around. Find "was a green parrot" at the end first. Then read: "A green parrot was sitting on a branch outside ..."

sentences.context: And with his giant hands, he held Jack and Annie as if they were two kittens.
sentences.simple: He held Jack and Annie in his very big hands, as easily as you hold two little cats.
sentences.main: He held Jack and Annie.

parts.meaning: With his very big hands,
he held the two children

parts.text: as if they were two kittens.
parts.meaning: like they were two small cats.

sentences.grammar: "As if" means "like". It shows how easy it was for him: the children were as small and weak as kittens to him.

sentences.context: They can rot there till they’re ready to tell us how to find Kidd’s treasure!
sentences.simple: They can stay on the ship and suffer until they tell us where Kidd's treasure is!
sentences.main: They can rot there.

parts.meaning: They can stay there and suffer

parts.text: till they’re ready to tell us
parts.meaning: until they want to tell us
where we can find Captain Kidd's treasure!

sentences.grammar: "Till" means "until". "Rot" here does not really mean they will go bad like food; it means they will stay in a bad place for a long time.

sentences.context: It is said that he buried a treasure chest on a deserted island.
sentences.simple: People say that he put a box of treasure in the ground on an island with no people.
sentences.main: He buried a treasure chest.

parts.meaning: People say that
he put a box of gold in the ground
on an island where nobody lived.

sentences.grammar: "It is said that ..." means people tell this story, but we are not sure it is true. You can use it in your writing.

sentences.context: Then while all the pirates are digging, we’ll sneak up to the tree house.
sentences.simple: When the pirates are busy digging, we will go quietly to the tree house.
sentences.main: We’ll sneak up to the tree house.

parts.text: Then while all the pirates are digging,
parts.meaning: Then, at the time when the pirates are busy digging,

parts.text: we’ll sneak up to the tree house.
parts.meaning: we will quietly and secretly go to the tree house.

sentences.grammar: "While ..." tells you two things happen at the same time. This is Jack's plan, so he uses "will" (we'll).

sentences.context: “You’ll see a gale if I don’t get me gold today, by thunder!”
sentences.simple: If I don't get my gold today, I will be as angry as a storm!
sentences.main: You’ll see a gale.

parts.meaning: You will see a storm

parts.text: if I don’t get me gold today,
parts.job: When this will happen. "Me gold" = "my gold".
parts.meaning: if I do not get my gold today,
I really mean it!

sentences.grammar: Pinky says a gale (storm) is coming. Cap'n Bones answers that he will be the storm. "If ..., you'll see ..." is a warning.

sentences.context: He thought he knew her—knew her from somewhere else.
sentences.simple: He felt he knew the parrot from another place.
sentences.main: He thought he knew her.

parts.meaning: He felt that he knew the parrot

parts.job: The same idea again, with more.
parts.meaning: he knew her from another place.

sentences.grammar: The long line (—) adds more to the same idea. This is a clue: Polly is someone Jack has met before.

sentences.context: Then, in a great swirl of colors—in a blur of feathers and light—in a flapping and stretching and screeching—a new being took shape.
sentences.simple: Then, with turning colors, feathers, light, flapping and loud cries, a new person slowly appeared.
sentences.main: A new being took shape.

parts.meaning: Then,

parts.text: in a great swirl of colors
parts.meaning: in a big turning cloud of colors

parts.text: in a blur of feathers and light
parts.meaning: in moving feathers and light that you could not see clearly

parts.text: in a flapping and stretching and screeching
parts.meaning: with wings flapping, the body stretching, and loud cries
a new person slowly appeared.

sentences.grammar: Jump over the three "in a ..." parts first: "Then a new being took shape." They all tell you how it happened. "Being" here means a living thing.

sentences.context: You are lucky to be born in a time with so many books.
sentences.simple: You are lucky because you live in a time when there are so many books.
sentences.main: You are lucky.

parts.meaning: You have good luck

parts.text: to be born in a time with so many books.
parts.meaning: because you live at a time with lots of books.

sentences.grammar: "Lucky to ..." tells you why someone is lucky. In Morgan's time, books were copied by hand, so there were very few.

sentences.context: Sometimes I want to visit the scenes in the pictures. So all the bookmarks mark places I wish to go.
sentences.simple: I want to go to the places in the pictures. The bookmarks show the places I want to visit.
sentences.main: The bookmarks mark places.

parts.text: Sometimes I want to visit the scenes in the pictures.
parts.meaning: Sometimes I want to go to the places I see in the pictures.

parts.text: So all the bookmarks mark places I wish to go.
parts.job: What she did because of that.
parts.meaning: So every bookmark shows a place I want to go to.

sentences.grammar: Here "mark" means "to show a place". "Places I wish to go" = "places that I want to go to".

sentences.context: “So when I point to a picture and make the wish, the tree house takes me there.”
sentences.simple: When I point to a picture and wish, the tree house carries me to that place.
sentences.main: The tree house takes me there.

parts.text: So when I point to a picture
parts.meaning: When I put my finger on a picture
and say "I wish ...",

parts.text: the tree house takes me there.
parts.meaning: the tree house carries me to that place.

sentences.grammar: "When ..." gives the two things she must do first. Then the main part tells you what happens. This is how the magic works.

sentences.context: “Then you picked up a book, Jack. And because you love books so much, you caused my magic spell to work.”
sentences.simple: Then you picked up a book. You love books so much that you made my magic work.
sentences.main: You caused my magic spell to work.

parts.text: Then you picked up a book, Jack.
parts.meaning: Then you picked up a book.

parts.text: And because you love books so much,
parts.meaning: Because you love books very much,

parts.text: you caused my magic spell to work.
parts.meaning: you made my magic work.

sentences.grammar: "Because ..." gives the reason first. "Cause something to work" means "make it work".

sentences.context: “You can’t imagine my dismay when you started to take off for dinosaur times.
sentences.simple: You cannot think how shocked I was when you began to go to the time of dinosaurs.
sentences.main: You can’t imagine my dismay.

parts.meaning: You cannot think how worried and shocked I was

parts.text: when you started to take off for dinosaur times.
parts.meaning: when you began to go to the time of dinosaurs.

sentences.grammar: "You can't imagine ..." means it was very, very strong. "Take off for" a place means leave for it.

a bunch of.meaning: A lot of; a group of.
a bunch of.example: a mummy box, and a bunch of cows

a series of.meaning: Several things of the same kind, one after another.
a series of.example: A series of tiny pictures were carved into the stone.
a series of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

a sigh of relief.meaning: A long breath out when a worry is over.
a sigh of relief.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

about to.meaning: "Be about to do something" means to be going to do it very soon.
about to.example: The sun was about to set.
about to.usageNote: A very common phrase. Good to learn.

as fast as one can.example: they ran as fast as they could
as fast as one can.usageNote: A very common phrase. Good to learn.

as if.meaning: In a way that makes you think something is true.
as if.example: it seemed as if she was swimming in front of him
as if.usageNote: A very common phrase. Good to learn.

as well.example: Jack heard another sound as well.
as well.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

aye aye.meaning: "Yes, sir! I will do it!" Sailors say it to the captain.
aye aye.usageNote: Old or pirate talk. You only need to understand it.

back and forth.meaning: First one way and then the other way, again and again.
back and forth.example: Jack rocked back and forth in the saddle.
back and forth.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

back away.meaning: To move slowly backward, away from something.
back away.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

be made up of.example: The floor of the room was made up of stones.

be supposed to.meaning: Should; it is the rule. "We're not supposed to be here" means we should not be here.
be supposed to.example: We’re not supposed to be up here.
be supposed to.usageNote: A very common phrase. Good to learn.

believe in.meaning: To believe that something is real or good.
believe in.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

belong to.meaning: If a thing belongs to you, it is yours.
belong to.example: We don’t know who it belongs to
belong to.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

bend over.meaning: To move the top of your body down.
bend over.example: He bent over and dragged the helmet over his head.

bit by bit.meaning: Slowly, a little at a time.
bit by bit.example: Jack inched down, bit by bit.
bit by bit.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

blow a kiss.meaning: To kiss your hand and then blow on it toward someone.
blow a kiss.example: Annie blew a kiss at him.

book of the dead.meaning: In ancient Egypt, a long paper with magic words that people put in a tomb to help the dead person in the next life.
book of the dead.example: Someone must find my Book of the Dead
book of the dead.usageNote: You only need to understand it in this book.

by thunder.meaning: An old cry to show you are angry or mean what you say.
by thunder.usageNote: Old or pirate talk. You only need to understand it.

can't help oneself.meaning: You cannot stop yourself from doing something, even if you know you should not.
can't help oneself.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

carry off.meaning: To take something away, often to steal it.
carry off.example: Tomb robbers often carried off the treasure
carry off.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

catch one's eye.meaning: If something catches your eye, you suddenly notice it.
catch one's eye.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

catch your breath.meaning: To stop breathing for a moment because you are surprised or excited. It can also mean to rest after running.
catch your breath.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

check on.meaning: To look at something to see if it is right or OK.
check on.example: I’ve got to check on something first.

clear away.meaning: To take something away so a place is clear.
clear away.example: Then the rain cleared away more sand.
clear away.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

clear your throat.meaning: To make a small cough before you speak.
clear your throat.example: He cleared his throat and said
clear your throat.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

close by.example: So there must be more mothers close by.
close by.usageNote: Good to learn. "Nearby" means the same.

come along.meaning: To go with someone; or to arrive.
come along.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

come at.meaning: To move toward someone to attack them.
come at.example: if a mean dog comes at you

come into focus.meaning: To become clear so you can see it well.
come into focus.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

come on.meaning: You say it to make someone hurry, or to ask them to come with you.
come on.example: Come on, Annie! It’s time to go home!
come on.usageNote: A very common phrase in talk.

forms: brought his horse to a stop
come to a stop.example: When they came to a stop

come to the rescue.meaning: To come and help someone in danger.
come to the rescue.example: A black cat had come to the rescue there.
come to the rescue.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

count on.meaning: To be sure that something will happen. "Don't count on it" means "I don't think so".
count on.usageNote: Common. Also "count on someone": to trust someone to help.

cut it out.usageNote: Common in talk, a little rude.

dry out.meaning: To become dry, or to make something dry.
dry out.example: First it was dried out with salt.
dry out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

fade away.meaning: To slowly become less clear until it is gone.
fade away.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

fall silent.meaning: To stop talking or making a sound.
fall silent.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

feel around for.meaning: To look for something with your hands, without seeing it.
feel around for.example: He felt around for the pencil

feel one's way.meaning: To move slowly and carefully, using your hands, because you cannot see well.
feel one's way.example: felt his way down the small ladder

feel your way.meaning: To move slowly, touching things with your hands, because you cannot see.
feel your way.example: They felt their way through the darkness.
feel your way.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

feet first.meaning: With your feet going before the rest of your body.
feet first.example: I’m going to have to go feet first

figure out.meaning: To think about something until you understand it.
figure out.example: Now he was trying to figure them out.
figure out.usageNote: A very common phrase. Good to learn.

find out.meaning: To learn a fact that you did not know.
find out.example: And find out if the magic person is a fact.
find out.usageNote: A very common phrase. Good to learn.

find your voice.meaning: To be able to speak again after being too surprised or afraid.
find your voice.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

find yourself.meaning: To see that you are in a place you did not plan.
find yourself.example: He found himself at the top of some stairs.
find yourself.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

fix one's eyes on.meaning: To look at someone or something for a long time and not look away.
fix one's eyes on.example: The creature fixed his eyes on Annie.
fix one's eyes on.usageNote: Good to understand. Here "fix" does not mean "repair".

flick off.meaning: To turn off a light quickly with your finger.

flip through.meaning: To turn the pages of a book quickly.

for real.meaning: Really; in real life, not just in a picture or a game.
for real.example: I wish I could see a Pteranodon for real.
for real.usageNote: Common in talk, more for young people.

for sure.example: he knew for sure that their trip
for sure.usageNote: A very common phrase. Good to learn.

forget it.meaning: Stop trying; it is no use. Or: do not worry about it.

get away from.meaning: To escape from someone or something.
get away from.example: How could they get away from him?
get away from.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

get back.meaning: Move back! Go away from the danger.
get back.usageNote: Common. It can also mean "return home".

get down.meaning: To go low, close to the floor, so you are safe.
get down.usageNote: Common. It can also mean "come down from a high place".

get dressed.usageNote: A very common phrase. Good to learn.

get out of.meaning: To leave a place, often a bad or dangerous place.
get out of.example: We have to get out of here
get out of.usageNote: A very common phrase. Good to learn.

get to him.meaning: To make him feel something strongly, so he wants to do it.
get to him.example: She sure knew how to get to him.

go ahead.meaning: Yes, start now; you can do it.
go ahead.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

go on.example: I want to see what’s really going on, Jack.
go on.usageNote: "What's going on?" is very common. It means "What is happening?"

go out.meaning: (Of a fire or light) To stop burning or shining.
go out.usageNote: Common. It also means "leave the house".

go too far.meaning: To do more than is OK or safe.
go too far.example: But this was going too far.

guess what.meaning: Words you say before you tell someone surprising news.
guess what.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

had better.meaning: You should do it, or something bad may happen. "We better not" means "We should not".
had better.usageNote: Very common in talk. People often drop "had" and just say "better", like Jack does.

hang it.meaning: An old angry cry, like "Oh no!" or "I am angry!"
hang it.usageNote: Old or pirate talk. You only need to understand it.

here goes.meaning: You say it just before you try something new or a little scary.

here we go.meaning: We are starting now! People say it when something exciting begins.
here we go.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

high on your list.meaning: Very important to you; one of the things you like most.
high on your list.example: Pyramids were high on his list of favorite things.
high on your list.usageNote: You only need to understand it in this book.

hit the ground.meaning: To drop down flat on the ground very quickly, to hide or be safe.

hold on.usageNote: Also used on the phone: "Hold on" means "wait a moment".

hold on to.meaning: To hold something tightly so you do not fall or lose it.
hold on to.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

hold one's breath.meaning: To stop breathing for a short time, often because you are afraid or excited.
hold one's breath.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

hold out.meaning: To put your hand or a thing out toward someone.
hold out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

hold your breath.meaning: To stop breathing for a short time, often because you are afraid or waiting.
hold your breath.example: Jack held his breath as he backed away.
hold your breath.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

hook into.meaning: To join or connect with something.
hook into.example: Somehow you hooked right into my magic.
hook into.usageNote: You only need to understand it in this book.

in a daze.meaning: Not able to think clearly, because you are surprised or tired.
in a daze.example: In a daze, Jack unzipped his backpack.

in awe.meaning: With great wonder and a little fear, because something is very big or beautiful.
in awe.example: He held his breath as he stared in awe.

in big trouble.meaning: In a very bad or dangerous situation.
in big trouble.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

in buckets.meaning: (of rain) Very, very heavily; a lot.
in buckets.usageNote: Good to know. People also say "It is raining cats and dogs."

in case.example: In case we want to come right back here.
in case.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

in fact.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

in full view of.meaning: Where someone can see you very clearly.
in full view of.example: In full view of the Triceratops!

in shock.meaning: Very surprised and upset, so you cannot think or move.
in shock.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

in the distance.example: A deep sound rumbled in the distance.
in the distance.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

in the world.meaning: Used to show surprise. "What in the world ...?" means "What ... ? I really do not know!"
in the world.example: What in the world was she saying?
in the world.usageNote: Common in talk. In other places, "in the whole world" just means "of all places".

it is said that.meaning: People say that ... (but we are not sure it is true).
it is said that.example: It is said that he buried a treasure chest
it is said that.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

jolly roger.meaning: The black flag of pirates, with a skull and crossbones.
jolly roger.usageNote: You only need to understand it in this book.

just in time.meaning: Just before it was too late.
just in time.example: He grabbed them just in time.
just in time.usageNote: A very common phrase. Good to learn.

just then.example: Just then a giant shadow covered Jack.
just then.usageNote: Common in stories. Good to learn.

king arthur.meaning: A famous king in old English stories, with his knights of the Round Table.
king arthur.example: Have you ever heard of King Arthur?
king arthur.usageNote: You only need to understand it in this book.

lead the way.meaning: To go first so others can follow you.
lead the way.example: And he led the way through the ferns.
lead the way.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

leave alone.meaning: To stop hurting or troubling someone.
leave alone.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

let go.meaning: To stop holding someone or something; to let a person leave.
let go.example: “Let go!” Annie shouted into his face.
let go.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

let out.meaning: To make a sound, like a cry or a long breath.
forms: let out a sad tuba sound
let out.example: The dinosaur let out a sad tuba sound.

lie down.meaning: To put your body flat on the floor or a bed.
lie down.example: the guards lay down on the wet floor
lie down.usageNote: A very common phrase. Note: "lay down" here is the past of "lie down".

light as a feather.meaning: Very, very light; not heavy at all.
light as a feather.usageNote: A common way to say something is very light.

look around.meaning: To look at the things in a place.
look around.usageNote: A very common phrase. Good to learn.

look up.meaning: 1. To look for a fact in a book. 2. To raise your eyes.
look up.example: “I’ll look it up.” Jack grabbed the dinosaur book.
look up.usageNote: A very common phrase. Good to learn.

lose one's balance.meaning: To start to fall because you cannot stand still and straight.
lose one's balance.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

lose your mind.example: seemed to have lost their minds
lose your mind.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

make a face.meaning: To move your face in a funny or unhappy way, to show you do not like something.
make a face.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

make friends with.meaning: To start to be friends with someone.
make friends with.example: She was always trying to make friends with animals.
make friends with.usageNote: A very common phrase. Good to learn.

make it.meaning: To get to a safe place; to do something hard and come through it OK.
make it.usageNote: Very common in talk. Good to learn.

me neither.meaning: You say it to agree with something that is "not": "I can't sleep." "Me neither" means "I can't sleep too".
me neither.usageNote: Very common in talk. Good to learn.

meet thy doom.meaning: To die; to have a terrible end.
meet thy doom.usageNote: Old or pirate talk. You only need to understand it.

morgan le fay.meaning: A woman who can do magic in the old stories of King Arthur. She is the M person.
morgan le fay.example: My name is Morgan le Fay.
morgan le fay.usageNote: You only need to understand it in this book.

much less.meaning: And surely not. "He couldn't see the moat, much less a crocodile" means a crocodile was even harder to see.

next door.meaning: In the house or room just beside yours.
next door.example: Next door was their neighbor’s black dog, Henry.
next door.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

next life.meaning: In ancient Egypt, people believed a person lives a new life after death.
next life.example: I need it to go on to the Next Life.
next life.usageNote: You only need to understand it in this book.

no doubt.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

no idea.meaning: "I had no idea" means "I did not know at all".
no idea.example: I had no idea it would ever be discovered.
no idea.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

no sign of.meaning: You cannot see someone or something anywhere.
no sign of.example: No sign of his mom or dad.
no sign of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

no such thing as.meaning: It is not real; it does not exist.
no such thing as.example: There’s no such thing as ghosts
no such thing as.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

no use.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

no way.usageNote: Very common in informal talk. Good to learn.

nowhere in sight.meaning: You cannot see it or them anywhere.
nowhere in sight.example: The ghost-queen was nowhere in sight.
nowhere in sight.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

of course.meaning: Yes, surely. You say it when the answer is clear.
of course.usageNote: A very common phrase. Good to learn.

oh brother.meaning: Words that show you are unhappy or think something will be a problem.
oh brother.usageNote: Informal American talk. It has nothing to do with a real brother.

oh dear.meaning: Words that show you are a little surprised or worried.
oh dear.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

oh man.meaning: Words that show a strong feeling: surprise, worry or wonder.
oh man.usageNote: Jack says this all the time. Informal American talk.

on either side.meaning: On both sides; on the left and on the right.

on her way.example: was the ghost-queen finally on her way to the Next Life?
on her way.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

one at a time.meaning: First one, then the next one; not all together.
one at a time.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

one by one.example: One by one, the guards lay down on the wet floor.
one by one.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

pay attention to.example: But Annie wasn’t paying attention to Jack.
pay attention to.usageNote: A very common phrase. Good to learn.

peanut butter.meaning: A soft brown food made from peanuts. People put it on bread.
peanut butter.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

pick up.meaning: 1. To lift something up with your hand. 2. "The wind picked up" means the wind got stronger.
pick up.example: The wind picked up. It was whistling now.
pick up.usageNote: A very common phrase with many meanings. Good to learn.

pipe up.meaning: To suddenly say something, often in a high voice.
pipe up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

pitch dark.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

poke one's head out.meaning: To put your head out of a window or door for a short time to look.
poke one's head out.example: Annie poked her head out of the tree house window

pretend stuff.meaning: Games and stories that are not real; things you imagine.

pull out.meaning: To take something out of a bag or pocket.
pull out.usageNote: A very common phrase. Good to learn.

put a spell on.meaning: To use magic to make something or someone change.
put a spell on.example: I placed a spell on the tree house
put a spell on.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

put away.meaning: To put something back in its place, or where it is kept.
put away.usageNote: A very common phrase. Good to learn.

quit it.usageNote: Common in talk between children. A little rude.

race you.meaning: A child's way to say "Let's run, and see who gets there first!"
race you.usageNote: Children say it all the time in play.

ready set go.meaning: Words said just before a race starts.
ready set go.usageNote: Good to know. Chinese races use similar words.

remind of.meaning: To make someone think of another person or thing because they are alike.
remind of.example: You remind me too much of myself.
remind of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

roll up.meaning: To turn the ends of your trousers or sleeves up so they are shorter.
roll up.example: Then he rolled up his jeans.
roll up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

run down.meaning: (Of a battery) To lose its power slowly.

scoop up.meaning: To pick something up quickly with your arms or hands.

see for yourself.meaning: To look at it with your own eyes.
see for yourself.example: You have to see for yourself.
see for yourself.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

set down.usageNote: Good to understand. "Put down" means the same.

set off.example: He and Annie set off for the palm trees.
set off.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

shake like a leaf.meaning: To shake a lot, like a leaf in the wind. People often say it when someone is very afraid.
shake like a leaf.example: The tree house shook like a leaf.

shut up.example: “Shut up!” Cap’n Bones roared at his men.
shut up.usageNote: Common but rude. Do not say it to people.

skull and crossbones.meaning: A picture of a skull with two bones under it, like an X. It is the sign of pirates, or of danger and poison.
skull and crossbones.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

slam shut.meaning: To close very hard and fast, with a loud noise.

sort of.example: he sort of wanted to take a peek himself
sort of.usageNote: Very common in talk. In writing, use "a little".

spread out.meaning: To open wide so it covers a big space.
spread out.example: His giant wings were spread out on either side of him.

stand for.meaning: If a letter stands for a word, it is a short way to write that word.
stand for.example: You think M stands for magic person?
stand for.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

stand guard.meaning: To stand near something and watch it to keep it safe.
stand guard.example: All standing guard around the nests.

start up.meaning: To begin to climb or go up.

stay afloat.meaning: To stay on top of the water and not go down.

step by step.example: Step by step, she and Jack walked
step by step.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

stick out.meaning: To come out past the edge of something, so you can see it.
stick out.example: He noticed bookmarks were sticking out of many of them.
stick out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

sure enough.meaning: Just as you thought; yes, it was true.
sure enough.example: Sure enough. There was their white wooden house

swallow up.meaning: To cover something so it cannot be seen.
swallow up.example: Everything had been swallowed up by the thick, soupy darkness.

switch on.meaning: To turn on a light or machine.
switch on.usageNote: Good to learn. "Turn on" means the same.

take a deep breath.meaning: To breathe in a lot of air, often to make yourself calm or brave.
take a deep breath.usageNote: A very common phrase. Good to learn.

take a peek.meaning: To look quickly at something, often secretly.
take a peek.example: I’m going to take a peek.
take a peek.usageNote: Good to understand. "Take a look" is more common.

take care of.meaning: 1. To look after someone. 2. Here the guard means "to deal with and punish" someone.
take care of.example: He knows how to take care of thieves.
take care of.usageNote: A very common phrase. Most often it means "look after".

take notes.meaning: To write down short things you see or hear, so you can remember them.
take notes.usageNote: A very common phrase for school. Good to learn.

take off.meaning: 1. To run away fast; to leave. 2. To leave the ground and start to fly. 3. To remove clothes or a bag.
take off.example: she took off down the hill
take off.usageNote: A very common phrase with many meanings. Good to learn.

take seriously.meaning: To think that someone means what they say.
take seriously.example: They didn’t take her seriously at all.
take seriously.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

take up the cry.meaning: To start shouting the same words as someone else.
take up the cry.example: The pirates took up the cry.
take up the cry.usageNote: You only need to understand it in this book.

tear through.meaning: To look through something very fast. (Here "tear" sounds like "bear".)
tear through.example: He grabbed it and tore through it

tear yourself away.meaning: To make yourself leave something you like a lot.
tear yourself away.example: But Jack couldn’t tear himself away.
tear yourself away.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

that was close.meaning: Something bad almost happened, but it did not. ("Close" sounds like "dose".)
that was close.usageNote: Common in talk. Good to learn.

the coast is clear.meaning: It is safe now; no one can see you or hurt you.
the coast is clear.usageNote: Common, often in a joke. Jack says it short: "Coast clear."

the next thing one knew.meaning: Suddenly, very fast, before you understood what was happening.
the next thing one knew.example: The next thing he knew, his helmet was yanked off.

throw up.meaning: To have food come back up out of your mouth because you feel sick or very afraid.

too late.meaning: After the right time; it cannot be stopped now.
too late.example: Too late. The big dinosaur had spotted Annie.

tread water.meaning: To stay up in deep water by moving your legs and arms, without swimming forward.

treasure chest.meaning: A big strong box full of gold and jewels.
treasure chest.example: He found a picture of pirates burying a treasure chest.
treasure chest.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

turn off.meaning: To stop a light or machine with a switch.
turn off.usageNote: A very common phrase. Good to learn.

turn on.meaning: To start a light or machine with a switch.
turn on.usageNote: A very common phrase. Good to learn.

turn out.meaning: To be found to be something in the end.
turn out.example: But it just turns out to be the sunlight
turn out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

turn over to.meaning: To give a person to someone who will decide what to do with them, like the police.
turn over to.example: Then turn them over to the Duke

up to.meaning: As much as; not more than.
up to.example: A helmet alone could weigh up to forty pounds.
up to.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

wander off.meaning: To walk slowly away from a place.

watch out.meaning: Be careful! You say it when something bad may happen.
watch out.example: Watch out, Jack! The monster’s coming!
watch out.usageNote: A very common phrase. Good to learn.

who cares.meaning: It is not important; I don't care.
who cares.example: “Who cares? We have to go!” said Annie.
who cares.usageNote: Common in talk, a little rude.

wipe out.meaning: To kill or destroy all of something.

write down.meaning: To write something on paper so you remember it.
write down.example: he started to write down this new fact
write down.usageNote: A very common phrase. Good to learn.

you're nuts.meaning: You are crazy; what you say or do is silly.
you're nuts.example: “You’re nuts. He can’t talk,” said Jack.
you're nuts.usageNote: Common, friendly talk. Do not say it to a teacher!
